entry.heading: Chainsaw Man (Tatsuki Fujimoto)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life here is an ordinary one: food, a home, people to eat with, and the freedom to choose your own wants instead of having them chosen for you.

delivery.evidence: Inferred from the entry's summaries; no review addresses preachiness.
delivery.note: Its ideas come through absurd, violent events and the characters' choices rather than stated morals.

personified.ideology: A better world through total control
Simple desires and living day to day

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Absurdism, Pagan/occult imagery, Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued), Hedonism (explored).

entry.heading: Jujutsu Kaisen (Gege Akutami)
entry.label: From summaries

delivery.evidence: Inferred from the entry's summaries; no review addresses preachiness.
delivery.note: Rival philosophies are voiced by antagonists in battle dialogue, while Yuji answers them by action rather than argument.

personified.ideology: Strength and pleasure are all that matter
Souls are only shapes; nothing has meaning

entry.dominant: Dharmic (Buddhist) imagery, Pagan/occult (Japanese folk religion), Existentialism, Might makes right (critiqued), Nihilism (critiqued). The labels below are this entry's framing unless a source is named.

entry.heading: Berserk
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is a stubborn struggle: you keep fighting against fate, cruelty and your own rage, and you choose to protect the people beside you rather than sacrifice them for a dream.

content.framing: Mixed: sexual violence shown as atrocity with lasting consequences; critics dispute how it is drawn

delivery.evidence: A.V. Club (Jones): "It is not concerned with right from wrong." No review in the entry calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its ideas about struggle, ambition and fate are carried by action and imagery, and the unfinished story gives no final verdict.

personified.ideology: A dream that justifies any sacrifice

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Might makes right (critiqued), Pagan/occult (explored), Nihilism (explored and resisted), Christian (critiqued as institution, echoed in themes).

entry.heading: One Piece
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is a free life spent chasing your own dream, side by side with friends who would die for you, and never bowing to anyone who claims the right to own other people.

content.framing: Shown with consequences; condemned when villains do it
Played as comedy; sexual coercion condemned

content.raw: 3 (manga); higher in the anime dub and live action

content.framing: Alcohol and tobacco shown casually; drugs condemned

delivery.evidence: Inferred from the entry's summaries; no review addresses preachiness.
delivery.note: Its anti-tyranny stance is stated openly in arc climaxes, while the Marines range from decent officers to fanatics.

personified.ideology: Absolute Justice, order at any price

lenses.label: Might makes right
lenses.stance: Critiqued, though power decides most fights

entry.dominant: Libertarianism (liberty and anti-authoritarianism), Classical virtue ethics (loyalty and courage), Communitarianism (the crew and freed peoples), and a critique of Collectivism/authoritarianism. "Anti-authoritarian" is drawn from Wikipedia's account of the themes. The labels Critical theory, Expressive individualism, Communitarianism, Pragmatism and Confucian ethics are our framing, not any source's.

entry.heading: Attack on Titan (Shingeki no Kyojin)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is lived freely and for the people you love, but freedom pursued through violence spreads the hatred it means to escape; the story asks the reader to keep looking for understanding even when the world is cruel.

delivery.evidence: New Republic (Amin) and Berkeley Political Review read a clear warning about fascism; no review in the entry calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Characters state their positions on freedom, revenge and peace openly, and the story gives each side a hearing before its ending.

personified.ideology: Freedom for his people at any cost
Anti-natalist mercy: end suffering by ending births
A child soldier shaped by state propaganda

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Utilitarianism, Might makes right (critiqued), Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued), Expressive individualism (critiqued), Nihilism (critiqued).

entry.heading: Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is lived for others. You protect the weak, honor the dead, keep promises, and pass your will to the next generation. A long or powerful life bought by harming others is worth nothing.

delivery.evidence: Tallon (Christian Research Journal): "Humanizing is the goal, instead of demonizing." No review in the entry calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its messages about compassion and duty are spoken in Tanjiro's lines and shown through the demons' backstories.

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Confucian ethics, Communitarianism, Dharmic (Buddhist), Traditionalism, Stoicism.

series.title: Tokyo Ghoul
series.native: 東京喰種 トーキョーグール

entry.title: Tokyo Ghoul
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.life_message: It holds up keeping one's humanity and care for others when the world forces a choice between two hostile sides.

content.note: Ghouls kill and eat people; brutal fights and torture (Wikipedia on cannibalism and killings; AniList Cannibalism 88%, Gore 83%, Torture).
Horror tone, body horror and the threat of being eaten (Wikipedia; AniList Body Horror, Survival).
Little romance; no notable sexual content listed (to verify).
Identity crisis and trauma after torture (to verify).
Anime and game franchise; no product focus.

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Might makes right (critiqued), Critical theory

delivery.evidence: ANN's vol. 1 review calls one book-within-the-book analogy a bit heavy-handed but finds the humanity question carried by Kaneki's situation.

personified.ideology: keeping one's humanity between two hostile sides

delivery.note: Its question about humanity is carried mainly by Kaneki's position between ghouls and humans, with one pointed literary analogy.

entry.heading: Goodnight Punpun
entry.label: From summaries

delivery.evidence: Asano (ANN interview, 2018) says the work offers no answers, only questions.
delivery.note: The series avoids stated morals and leaves most of its verdicts open.

personified.ideology: Frank friendship and creative work as a reason to go on

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Nihilism (explored, not affirmed), Absurdism, Dharmic (Buddhist) by echo, Postmodernism.

series.title: My Hero Academia
series.native: 僕のヒーローアカデミア

entry.heading: My Hero Academia (Boku no Hero Academia)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is spent helping others without being asked, even at cost to yourself; and real heroism means reaching out to save the person no one else will, including the "villain".

content.framing: Mixed: Mineta's behavior is mostly condemned or punished by classmates; adult heroine costumes are neutral

delivery.evidence: Anime Feminist's Mo Black reads its politics as conservative; Plugged In praises its self-sacrifice message; neither calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Villains such as Shigaraki and Stain state their grievances against hero society directly, and the story answers mainly through Deku.

personified.ideology: A society that failed a child deserves destruction
Only true heroes deserve the name

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Communitarianism, Might makes right (critiqued), Christian (redemptive) themes, Critical theory (contested), Traditionalism.

entry.heading: One-Punch Man
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A hero is someone who keeps helping people and keeps fighting, without needing praise, rank or even a challenge. Strength, fame and status are empty if they are the goal. Doing the right thing for its own sake is what counts.

content.framing: Neutral (comic) to Shown with consequences (late arcs)
Neutral (played for gags and pin-up appeal)

delivery.evidence: Christ and Pop Culture's Kloosterman draws a lesson on faithful effort; Common Sense Media finds "very little" positive messaging; neither calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its themes arrive mostly through parody and anticlimax rather than stated lessons.

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Classical virtue ethics, Absurdism, Might makes right (critiqued), Stoicism.

entry.heading: Vagabond
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is a long road from killing to living: strength that serves only the self is empty, and the warrior grows by facing fear, accepting limits, and learning to belong to the earth and to other people.

content.framing: Mixed: some encounters shown as exploitative or empty; framing to verify

delivery.evidence: The Japan Times traces Musashi from "solitary brute to thoughtful hermit"; no review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its Zen-influenced ideas emerge mainly through Musashi's inner monologue and duels rather than stated lessons.

personified.ideology: Wisdom that has let go of winning
Family honor turned into a grudge

entry.dominant: Dharmic (Zen Buddhist), Existentialism, Classical virtue ethics, with Might makes right present but critiqued.

entry.heading: Spy x Family (Tatsuya Endo)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is building a family, even an imperfect or "fake" one, and protecting the peace that lets children grow up without war.

content.frequency: Occasional; heavy in a few arcs
content.framing: Shown with consequences (Yor's work) / Neutral (spy action)

delivery.evidence: Common Sense Media says "the most untraditional families can still be loving"; Plugged In calls it "primarily comedic"; neither calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its anti-war and family themes mostly sit under comedy, with occasional direct flashbacks such as Loid's childhood.

personified.ideology: Trade one's own life for peace

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Secular humanism, Communitarianism (family and peace first), Traditionalism (family form), anti-war Utilitarianism and Pragmatism.

entry.heading: Vinland Saga
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A true warrior needs no sword: a good life means turning from violence and revenge, facing one's guilt, and building, by hard and patient work, a place where no one is enslaved and no one is an enemy.

delivery.evidence: Common Sense Media lists messages on peace and revenge; Yukimura states his aim as "peace and compassion"; no review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Thors' line "A true warrior needs no sword" states the theme directly, and the later farm arcs build on it.

personified.ideology: Cunning survival in a rotten world

entry.dominant: Might makes right (critiqued), Christian (explored), Classical virtue ethics, Communitarianism, Secular humanism. The series' pacifism is not a listed lens; it is carried by the Christian, Dharmic and Secular humanism rows (my own framing).

entry.heading: The Promised Neverland
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life means refusing to accept a system that treats people as food, refusing to leave anyone behind, and refusing to answer cruelty with extermination: Emma wants everyone to live, enemies included, and she pays for it herself.

delivery.evidence: Common Sense Media says it "sides with the children and condemns the social system"; Shirai said it carries no specific message.
delivery.note: The three leads embody competing ethics of survival, and the plot tests each choice.

personified.ideology: Protect your own by removing the threat
Humans as stock for an elite

entry.dominant: Collectivism / authoritarianism (critiqued), Utilitarianism (critiqued), Secular humanism, Communitarianism, Classical virtue ethics. "Anti-exploitation" is not a listed lens; it is carried by the Critical theory and Marxism rows (my own framing).

entry.heading: Blue Lock
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: Find what only you can do and pursue it without apology. Hunger to win, honest self-analysis and constant adaptation make you great. Others are rivals to learn from and "devour," and teamwork is valuable when it serves the strongest individual.

content.frequency: Pervasive outside the book; recurring inside

delivery.evidence: Daily Campus calls it "propaganda" for hyper-competitive individualism; Common Sense Media says self-centered ego themes overshadow its positives.
delivery.note: Jinpachi Ego states the series' thesis in direct speeches, and the teamwork view is voiced mostly by players who are eliminated.

personified.ideology: Japan needs egoists; cooperation is weakness
The team-player style of passing over shooting

entry.dominant: Existentialism (self-creation), Expressive individualism, Pragmatism, Might makes right ("skill makes right"), Classical virtue ethics; Communitarianism and Confucian-style harmony critiqued.

entry.heading: Horimiya (HERO and Daisuke Hagiwara)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life comes from being known and accepted as you really are by a few people who choose you, and from caring for them in daily, ordinary ways; loneliness is the thing to be rescued from.

delivery.evidence: Silverman (ANN): "a private romance, based on the quiet feelings of the characters."
delivery.note: Its theme of hidden selves arises from everyday scenes, and no character stands for an opposing worldview.

entry.dominant: Expressive individualism, Communitarianism, Classical virtue ethics, Secular humanism.

entry.heading: Bleach
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is spent protecting the people you love, with your own heart as the guide even when authorities or gods are wrong; fear and death are part of life and give courage its meaning.

content.framing: Neutral (sword combat as the story's main action); Shown with consequences for atrocities

delivery.evidence: Inferred from the entry's summaries; no review addresses preachiness.
delivery.note: Its themes of resolve and loyalty against authority come through battles, and the villains' arguments are left partly unanswered.

personified.ideology: Protect loved ones and follow your own heart
Human will should take the empty place of heaven
A founder who gives and takes power by blood

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Classical virtue ethics, Pragmatism, a critique of Might makes right and of Collectivism/authoritarianism, with Dharmic and Shinto cosmology as setting. Labels other than those quoted from sources are our framing.

series.title: Kaguya-sama: Love is War

entry.heading: Kaguya-sama: Love Is War
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life takes the courage to be honest and vulnerable. Pride, mind games and fear of rejection keep people lonely; friends who see the real you, and love freely chosen, are worth more than wealth, status or family control.

delivery.evidence: Anime Feminist's Caitlin Moore reads the leads as "emotionally stunted" kids rather than a model; no review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its views on honesty and love come through comic mind games rather than stated lessons.

entry.dominant: Expressive individualism, Classical virtue ethics, Communitarianism, Secular humanism. Lens labels below are my own framing unless a source is named.

entry.heading: Tokyo Revengers
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is one where you never abandon your friends and never give up on someone, however far gone; real strength is heart and loyalty, not fists, and violence and revenge only feed a cycle that kills the people you love.

content.framing: Shown with consequences, but styled as cool

delivery.evidence: Nippon.com's Hotta Junji says it "in no way glorifies violent acts"; SLJ notes some could argue it glorifies gangs.
delivery.note: Its view of loyalty and the cycle of violence is carried by gang fights and the consequences of each time leap.

personified.ideology: Heart over strength; never give up on anyone

entry.dominant: Communitarianism (gang-as-family), Classical virtue ethics, Might makes right (critiqued), Existentialism, Confucian ethics.

entry.heading: Dandadan
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is lived with kindness toward people, spirits and outsiders alike: stand by your friends, protect the vulnerable, eat well after hard work, and do not let fear or other people's mockery decide who you are.

content.framing: Condemned (assaults, framed as villainy); Neutral (gags and fan service)

delivery.evidence: Reactor (Thomas): "Dandadan is a story about boundaries and respect." No review in the entry calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its themes of respect and found family come through comedy and horror episodes, and its predatory villains are condemned outright.

personified.ideology: Folk practice of coexistence between living and dead

entry.heading: Hunter x Hunter
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is a chosen adventure shared with friends. The story questions whether humans are better than the "monsters" they hunt, and it shows that strength, revenge and even goodness can become destructive when they turn obsessive.

delivery.evidence: Bobduh (Wrong Every Time): in the Chimera Ant arc no side is purely villainous. No review in the entry calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its moral questions come through plot turns and narration, and even its monsters are given a full hearing.

personified.ideology: Duty and gratitude, then whatever it takes

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Naturalism, Secular humanism, Might makes right (critiqued), Expressive individualism, Utilitarianism (explored).

entry.heading: Black Clover

entry.life_message: A good life is earned by effort, not birth: you refuse to give up, you lift up the people others look down on, and you build a family out of misfits.

People as things to be used

entry.heading: Komi Can't Communicate (Tomohito Oda)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is a life with others: anyone can be befriended if someone is patient with them, and the effort to reach out, however clumsy, is worth more than looking perfect.

delivery.evidence: ANN's Rebecca Silverman calls it "good-natured" with "a distinct lack of cruelty"; no review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Lessons about friendship and courage are carried by gag-chapter situations and character name puns.

personified.ideology: Ordinary kindness is enough to help

entry.heading: Kaiju No. 8
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: It is never too late: a good life keeps a childhood promise, does honest work well, and uses whatever power it has to protect others, inside a team that has learned to trust you.

delivery.evidence: That Sounds Awesome praises its "never too late" message; no review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its message about persistence is carried mainly by Kafka's situation as a 32-year-old latecomer.

personified.ideology: Persistence; it is never too late
Predation and absorbing others to grow

entry.heading: My Dress-Up Darling (Shinichi Fukuda)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life comes from loving what you love without shame, doing your craft with care, and being accepted by someone who admires the real you; mockery of a person's passions is the wrong to be undone.

content.framing: Endorsed (romance; Marin's open enjoyment of erotic media); Neutral (fan service gags)

delivery.evidence: ANN's Rebecca Silverman sums it up as "not being ashamed of what you love"; no review calls it preachy.

entry.heading: Death Note (Tsugumi Ohba and Takeshi Obata)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: The story shows a life spent claiming the power to judge others, and lets the reader watch where that leads. Ohba's own stated takeaway is: "Humans will all eventually die, so let's give it our all while we're alive" (Wikipedia, citing Ohba).

content.frequency: Constant (deaths every few chapters), mostly non-graphic

delivery.evidence: ANN's Briana Lawrence: "two opposing sides that both believe in the same thing: justice." No review in the entry calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Light and L argue openly about justice, and the story ends with Light's fall rather than a stated lesson.

personified.ideology: Justice by results; one genius may judge and kill
Rule of law, duty and honesty

entry.dominant: Utilitarianism (critiqued), Nihilism (explored), Might makes right (critiqued), Christian (explored, mostly as imagery and structure), Existentialism (explored).

entry.heading: Naruto (Masashi Kishimoto, 1999-2014)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is one where you never give up, earn the recognition of others through effort and loyalty, and break cycles of hatred by understanding and forgiving even your enemies.

delivery.evidence: Fans coined "Talk no Jutsu" for Naruto ending fights with speeches; TV Tropes calls the Pain arc ending a "Writer Cop Out."
delivery.note: Rival theories of peace are argued in speeches during fights and are usually resolved through Naruto's persuasion.

personified.ideology: Peace through shared pain and terror
A few must do terrible things for the many

entry.dominant: Communitarianism (village and "Will of Fire"), Dharmic (Buddhist cycle of hatred), Classical virtue ethics, Confucian ethics. Lens labels are this entry's framing unless a source is named. Wikipedia's Naruto article notes Confucian values (respect for teachers, filial duty, group over self); the other labels are this entry's own.

entry.heading: Hell's Paradise: Jigokuraku
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is an ordinary, chosen one: love that gives you a reason to live, honest bonds formed across enemy lines, and balance instead of extremes. Immortality bought by harvesting others, and obedience that empties out the self, are what the story rejects.

content.framing: Mixed: fan service neutral; coerced sex condemned

delivery.evidence: Inferred from the entry's summaries; no review addresses preachiness. Kotaku notes the violence is balanced by "humane compassion".
delivery.note: Themes of balance and humanity come through the Tao combat system and the convicts' and executioners' arcs.

personified.ideology: Doubt and compassion over rigid duty
Immortality and love turned to consuming attachment

lenses.lens: Taoist cosmology (added; not in the standard list)
lenses.label: Taoist cosmology (added; not in the standard list)

entry.dominant: Taoist cosmology (added row), Existentialism, Secular humanism, Dharmic (Buddhist), Transhumanism (critiqued), Critical theory.

entry.heading: A Silent Voice (Koe no Katachi)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is possible even after doing serious harm: own what you did, make amends, learn to listen, and accept that your life still has worth. Despair isolates; communication and friendship heal.

content.frequency: Frequent in v1 and v6, occasional elsewhere

delivery.evidence: SLJ calls its bullying portrait "so balanced that I not only understood why people bully"; Thunderword says the deaf girl lacks agency.
delivery.note: The anti-bullying message is shown through each character's own point of view rather than stated by a narrator, with explicit apologies at key turns.

personified.ideology: Atonement is possible and a harmful person's life still has worth
The victim is to blame for the group's troubles

entry.dominant: Secular humanism, Existentialism, Classical virtue ethics, Communitarianism.

entry.heading: Sakamoto Days
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is a peaceful, ordinary family life. Even a killer can start over, and he makes up for the lives he took by protecting and helping others, never by taking more.

content.framing: Shown with consequences (killing condemned; non-lethal force endorsed)

delivery.evidence: Common Sense Media quotes "It's never too late to start over"; no review opened calls it preachy; reviewers focus on comedy and action.
delivery.note: The no-kill message is carried by a running household rule and by action choices more than by speeches.

personified.ideology: Strength restrained for family; no killing
Sanctity of life; atonement by service
Violent revenge on an abusive system

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Communitarianism (family-first), Secular humanism, Traditionalism.

entry.heading: Dr. STONE
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is spent learning, building and sharing knowledge so that every person can live. Progress is slow, earned "ten billion percent" through work and cooperation, and it is passed down from parents to children.

delivery.evidence: Common Sense Media lists "the value of scientific progress" as a theme; LessWrong calls Tsukasa "value-based opposition." No review found calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The pro-science message is spoken openly in Senku's lines and Science Corner asides, while rival visions get a sympathetic hearing in Tsukasa and a thinner one in Ibara.

personified.ideology: "Pure youth" primitivism and purge of corrupt adults
Village priestess tradition and oral memory

entry.dominant: Secular humanism, Naturalism, Pragmatism; Might makes right and Collectivism/authoritarianism are strongly critiqued.

entry.heading: Dorohedoro (Q Hayashida)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is a shared meal, a loyal partner and a job you can keep. The world has no fair rulers, so you stick with your own people, keep your word to them, and laugh at the horror.

delivery.evidence: ANN's This Week in Anime calls it "a slapstick sitcom" in horror's skin; WSWS faults weak social analysis. No reviewer calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The series gives sorcerers, humans and devils each sympathetic and cruel members, and states no message outright.

personified.ideology: Loyalty and finding yourself through friends
Power as amusement; nothing is serious
Grievance of the exploited turned to slaughter

entry.dominant: Pagan/occult (as setting), Absurdism, Communitarianism (found family), Might makes right (as the world's rule).

entry.heading: Uzumaki: Spiral into Horror
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: The story promotes no clear good life. It shows a universe that is indifferent to people, where obsession, fear and even escape all lead to the same end. What survives longest is loyalty between people who love each other, and the story does not say that loyalty wins.

delivery.evidence: Silverman (ANN): "we can feel the inevitability of the outcome." No review found calls it preachy; reviewers stress mood over message.
delivery.note: Every response to the spiral (obsession, fear, flight, resistance, surrender) is given a sympathetic hearing and the same fate, so no view is made a strawman.

entry.dominant: Nihilism (cosmic, not moral), Absurdism, Existentialism, Pagan/occult (folk curse).

entry.heading: Goodbye, Eri (Tatsuki Fujimoto)
entry.label: From summaries

delivery.evidence: Reviewers praise its ambiguity; ANN says some may find it "pretentious" or "confusing"; none call it preachy.
delivery.note: Its ideas about grief, memory and fiction come through framing and ambiguous events rather than stated morals, and objections to Yuta's first film get a sympathetic voice.

personified.ideology: Facing loss through art and edited memory
Fiction as a way to be remembered
Self-image and career before her child
Respect for the dead over spectacle

entry.dominant: Postmodernism (fiction and reality), Existentialism (choosing to live), Expressive individualism (art as self), Absurdism (the explosion gag).

entry.title: Frieren: Beyond Journey’s End
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.life_message: Holds up paying attention to the people around you while you can, and carrying their kindness forward after they are gone.

content.note: Battles with demons and magic duels; some blood (to verify).
Death and loss are central but quiet; demons are menacing at times.
Light romantic teasing; no sexual content noted.
The priest Heiter drinks; mild (to verify).

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Communitarianism, Existentialism

delivery.evidence: Wikipedia: reviewers call it "serene and contemplative" with "deep thematic explorations of human nature".

personified.ideology: Learning to value fleeting human bonds

delivery.note: Its message about time and attention is left for readers to feel through episodic journeys; demons serve as a contrasting foil.

series.title: Three Days of Happiness
series.romaji: Jumyou wo Kaitotte Moratta. Ichinen ni Tsuki, Ichimanen de.
series.native: 寿命を買い取ってもらった。一年につき、一万円で。

entry.heading: Three Days of Happiness (Jumyou wo Kaitotte Moratta. Ichinen ni Tsuki, Ichimanen de.)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A life's worth is not its market price, its length or its achievements, but how it is lived and whom it is spent caring for; even a short, failed life can end in real happiness through love and kindness. The story's ending (both leads give up their remaining time to share three last days) leaves open whether that is fulfilment or surrender, and readers split on it.

delivery.evidence: MAL reviewers split: one says the ending is "a weirdly pessimistic way of shouting 'YOLO'"; another says it "reminds you" who you choose to be.
delivery.note: The theme of what a life is worth is stated openly through the appraisal and Miyagi's daily question, while the ending's meaning is left to the reader.

personified.ideology: A life's worth is measured by achievement and recognition, then by love given
Self-sacrifice and duty, paying for others at one's own cost
Despair and resentment turned into revenge
Lives can be priced by productivity and future happiness

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Secular humanism, Utilitarianism (explored), Consumerism (critiqued).

series.title: Witch Hat Atelier
series.native: とんがり帽子のアトリエ

entry.heading: Witch Hat Atelier
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life uses one's skills carefully and creatively to help others. Power must come with responsibility, mistakes must be owned, and no one should be shut out of learning because of their birth or body.

delivery.evidence: Beneath the Tangles: "Coco's coming of age never involves anything black and white." No review opened calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its ideas about access, responsibility and power come through plot dilemmas, with both the law and its rebels given reasons and faults.

personified.ideology: Protective care mixed with secret revenge; ends justify means
Magic should belong to everyone, at any cost
A duty to save people that overrides law
Order and enforcement of the Pact

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (prudence), Pragmatism, Critical theory (access and gatekeeping), Communitarianism, Progressivism, Pagan/occult (as fantasy witchcraft).

entry.heading: Land of the Lustrous
entry.label: From summaries

delivery.evidence: Reviewers praise its strangeness and ambiguity (Manga Bookshelf: "its own thing"); fans argue over who was right, Kongo or Phos.
delivery.note: The religious and philosophical ideas are carried by plot structure and symbol rather than speeches, and the story leaves most verdicts to the reader.

personified.ideology: Release into nothingness by any means

entry.dominant: Dharmic (Buddhist), Existentialism, Transhumanism (body and identity), Nihilism (explored), Communitarianism.

series.title: The Fragrant Flower Blooms With Dignity
series.romaji: Kaoru Hana wa Rin to Saku

entry.heading: The Fragrant Flower Blooms With Dignity (Saka Mikami)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life comes from seeing people as they are rather than as their label, from honest and patient kindness, and from working through fear and division together; love grows slowly and is tended.

delivery.evidence: MAL critics: characters lose essence avoiding miscommunication, apologizing constantly; CSM: "An important theme is how stereotypes are harmful."
delivery.note: The anti-prejudice theme is stated often in dialogue, but the prejudiced side, including Kikyo's teacher Toki, is given understandable reasons.

personified.ideology: Do not judge by appearance; gentle masculinity
Distrust of the privileged other school

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Communitarianism, Secular humanism.

entry.heading: Fullmetal Alchemist
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is lived within human limits. You accept loss, own your mistakes, work for what you get, give more than you take, and protect others instead of trying to become a god.

delivery.evidence: DVD Talk's Bobby Cooper first read the theme as anti-religious, then concluded Scar uses religion to justify murder (Wikipedia).
delivery.note: The series states its themes in dialogue about equivalent exchange and God, and shows them through consequences for each side.

personified.ideology: Equivalent exchange turned to giving more than you take; skepticism of gods
Ishvalan faith turned to revenge, then rebuilding
Religion as a tool of control

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Secular humanism (humble), Communitarianism, Transhumanism (critiqued), Collectivism / authoritarianism (critiqued), Pantheist / New Age.

entry.heading: Blue Period
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is one you choose and work for: find what moves you, put in the hours, be honest about yourself, and let others be who they are.

values.presence: Recurring (central in the exam arc, ch. 1-25)

delivery.evidence: ANN finds vol. 1 sometimes "how to"; reviewers praise Yuka's arc as serious. No opened review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The series argues through Yatora's inner monologue and art lessons, letting the mother, rivals and professors make real counterpoints.

entry.dominant: Expressive individualism, Existentialism, Classical virtue ethics, Secular humanism, Pragmatism.

entry.heading: Kingdom
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A worthy life is lived for a great dream larger than oneself: courage, loyalty to comrades and a just king, and the will to rise from nothing, spent in a war the story frames as the price of a lasting peace.

content.framing: Mixed: battlefield killing is heroic; massacres and torture are condemned by the heroes

delivery.evidence: MAL reviewers note chapters are often "mostly speeches"; one says the series "launders" the First Emperor's image; Lü Buwei and Li Mu get serious hearings.
delivery.note: Ying Zheng states the unification ideal in set-piece speeches and debates, while rivals like Lü Buwei and Li Mu are argued with rather than mocked.

personified.ideology: Unification by conquest and rule by law to end war
Coexistence of the states; defense of Zhao
Rage against the powerful; atrocity as method

entry.dominant: Collectivism/authoritarianism (affirmed in a benevolent form), Classical virtue ethics (affirmed), Might makes right (explored and partly affirmed), Utilitarianism, Confucian ethics (explored). Legalism, the Qin state philosophy Ying Zheng and Li Si stand for, is not on the list; it is carried by the Collectivism/authoritarianism and Pragmatism rows (my own framing).

series.title: Don't Toy With Me, Miss Nagatoro
series.native: イジらないで、長瀞さん

entry.heading: Don't Toy With Me, Miss Nagatoro
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is found by letting someone close enough to see your weak points, and growing braver through it. Confidence, honesty and showing your feelings are rewarded; hiding behind shyness or teasing is outgrown.

content.framing: Endorsed (romance and teasing); Neutral (fan service gags); Shown with consequences (the vol. 20 nude-drawing lie)
Endorsed early; softened; partly shown with consequences

delivery.evidence: ANN's Farris says the bullying premise becomes "practically an afterthought"; no review found calls the series preachy.
delivery.note: Its message about courage and honesty grows out of the romance itself, while the early teasing is presented with little critique inside the story.

personified.ideology: Quiet growth into courage and honesty
Teasing as a way of showing love

entry.dominant: Expressive individualism, Existentialism (self-making through risk), Hedonism (play and pleasure), Classical virtue ethics (courage and honesty, late).

entry.heading: Slam Dunk
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: Anyone can change: a hot-tempered delinquent and a bitter dropout find themselves through hard practice, humble basics and a team that takes them back. Talent matters only when it serves the team, and you are not finished until you give up.

content.framing: Played for comedy early; shown with consequences in the Mitsui arc

content.frequency: Pervasive outside the book; rare inside

delivery.evidence: ANN's Kimlinger calls it "a fun read" without depth early; Common Sense Media stresses teamwork and humility.
delivery.note: Lessons arrive through games and character turns, and rival teams' approaches are treated with respect.

personified.ideology: Bitterness and gang life, then repentance
Patient faith in players; never give up

entry.dominant: Communitarianism, Classical virtue ethics, Pragmatism; Might makes right and Nihilism critiqued.

entry.heading: The Climber (Kokou no Hito)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A life is worth living when you give all your strength to something, but no one can live entirely alone. The rope that ties climbers together, and in the end a family, is what brings a person back down the mountain.

delivery.evidence: ANN's Dee: unclear whether it critiques or endorses toxic masculinity. Reviewers praise visual metaphor; none call it preachy.
delivery.note: The message comes through visual metaphor, interior monologue and consequences rather than speeches.

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Expressive individualism (critiqued), Stoicism, Classical virtue ethics.

entry.heading: The Flowers of Evil
entry.label: From summaries

delivery.evidence: Reviewers praise that "everything is established through the natural flow of the aesthetics and scenes, not by anything being told to us" (Creamer).
delivery.note: The series gives each of its three teenagers' views a sympathetic voice and lets consequences, not statements, carry its verdicts.

personified.ideology: Nihilistic contempt for conformity; escape to "the other side"
Literature and creative work as a way to live
Romantic self-image as a Baudelairean outsider

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Nihilism (voiced, then moved past), Expressive individualism (explored), with secular humanism and a Dharmic echo in the recovery arc.

series.title: Homunculus
series.adult_reason: Homunculus: deep entry scores 9; likely Mature 18+ (publisher rating unconfirmed)

entry.heading: Homunculus
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: The series does not hold up a model of a good life. It shows people hiding guilt and trauma behind masks (money, rank, surgery, lies), and asks whether a person who has no self underneath the mask can be healed at all. Its answer, as summaries read it, is bleak: Nakoshi's search for himself ends in self-mutilation, a woman's death and a world in which every face is his own.

delivery.evidence: MAL reviewers call it "overexplained and pretentious" and "pseudo-philosophical"; Ito explains psychoanalytic theory on the page.
delivery.note: Ideas about trauma and the self are spelled out in dialogue, but the story never settles whether Nakoshi's visions are real.

personified.ideology: Scientific skepticism about the mind and the occult
A self made of surface: money, surgery, lies

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Postmodernism (identity as surface), Naturalism, Nihilism (explored).

series.title: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure Part 6: Stone Ocean
series.romaji: JoJo no Kimyou na Bouken: Stone Ocean
series.native: ジョジョの奇妙な冒険 ストーンオーシャン

entry.heading: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure Part 6: Stone Ocean
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is chosen, not fated: loyalty to family and friends, courage under unjust power, and sacrifice for the weak are worth more than the peace of a destiny imposed from above, and hope in an unknown future is part of being human.

delivery.evidence: TV Tropes calls Pucci the franchise's most well-intentioned villain; ANN's writers say the story answers his fate with hope and choice.
delivery.note: The villain argues his theology of fate in long speeches, and the story answers him through the heroes' choices and sacrifices rather than counter-sermons.

personified.ideology: Accepting a known fate is happiness; God's will as irresistible "gravity"
Will and hope against fate; sacrifice for others
Choice and justice can change fate
Victim of racism and fate who answers with vengeance

entry.dominant: Existentialism (affirmed), Classical virtue ethics (affirmed), Collectivism/authoritarianism and Stoic-style fatalism (critiqued through Pucci), Christian (explored through a villain), Critical theory and Feminism (explored).

entry.heading: Kagurabachi
entry.label: From summaries

content.framing: Mixed: revenge killing of villains endorsed early; atrocities and torture condemned; war violence shown with consequences

delivery.evidence: Reviewers focus on art, pacing and memes; none opened calls it preachy. Ch. 72 gives the "invaders" a human face.
delivery.note: Questions about revenge, war memory and a father's responsibility are carried by plot reveals and fights rather than speeches.

personified.ideology: Atonement by eliminating all who misused the blades
Exposing a national lie by violence
Might makes right; rule by one strongman

entry.dominant: Might makes right (critiqued), Classical virtue ethics, Traditionalism (filial and craft), Critical theory (war memory and state power).

series.title: Jujutsu Kaisen 0
series.romaji: Jujutsu Kaisen 0: Tokyo Toritsu Jujutsu Koutou Senmon Gakkou
series.native: 呪術廻戦 0 東京都立呪術高等専門学校

entry.heading: Jujutsu Kaisen 0 (Gege Akutami)
entry.label: From summaries

delivery.evidence: Reviewers praise Geto's presence but Otaku USA wanted more time for him; Beneath the Tangles calls his introduction muddied.
delivery.note: The love-as-curse theme is stated once in a line by Gojo and then shown through plot, while Geto's ideology gets little room in this volume.

personified.ideology: Sorcerers are superior; non-sorcerers should be exterminated
Love that releases; live to protect others
Possessive love that will not let go
Raise and protect the next generation

entry.dominant: Pagan/occult (Japanese folk religion and Shinto), Existentialism, Communitarianism, Dharmic (attachment and release), Might makes right (critiqued, through Geto's supremacy). Labels are this entry's framing unless a source is named.

series.title: Toilet-Bound Hanako-kun
series.native: 地縛少年 花子くん

entry.heading: Toilet-Bound Hanako-kun
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life treasures the people you have now, faces guilt and fate honestly, and refuses easy wishes that make someone else pay the price.

delivery.evidence: ANN calls it "a creepy old-fashioned fairy tale"; no review opened calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its warnings about wishes, guilt and sacrifice come through ghost-story plots, and the exorcist and coexistence views are both given reasons.

personified.ideology: Spirits must be exorcised; living and dead kept apart
Atonement through duty; ends justify means for the one he loves

entry.dominant: Pagan / occult (Japanese folk religion), Dharmic (Buddhist afterlife imagery), Existentialism (defying a written fate), Classical virtue ethics (loyalty and sacrifice).

series.title: Gantz
series.adult_reason: Gantz: Dark Horse rates it 18+; deep entry scores 10/10 mature content

entry.heading: Gantz
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is found in caring for particular people (a lover, a little brother, a friend) and protecting them, even in a universe that shows no sign of caring back. Selfishness, cruelty and pleasure-seeking are shown as both common and ugly; altruism is shown as rare and costly.

content.framing: Mixed: sexual assault is shown as vile; fan service and casual sex are not framed critically

delivery.evidence: Santos (ANN) says its killing dilemma sends "mixed messages"; a MAL reviewer calls the final arc unsubtle. No review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Most of its themes come through events, but the final arc states its cosmology through a long lecture by the beings behind Gantz.

personified.ideology: Meaning found through love and loyalty

personified.character: The beings behind Gantz (Room of Truth)
personified.ideology: Materialism; no God; souls without worth

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Nihilism, Naturalism, Secular humanism, Absurdism.

entry.heading: The Quintessential Quintuplets (Negi Haruba)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is built by honest effort, loyalty to family and the willingness to grow; love means choosing one person for life while keeping faith with everyone else you love.

content.framing: Endorsed (romance, ending in marriage); Neutral (fan-service gags)

delivery.evidence: The Guardian's Phil Hoad calls the film "stridently sentimental and moralistic"; most reviewers treat it as genre comfort food.
delivery.note: Its lessons on effort, family and fidelity come through exam arcs and sister conflicts, while the harem framing itself goes unexamined.

entry.dominant: Confucian ethics, Classical virtue ethics, Traditionalism, Communitarianism.

entry.heading: Soul Eater
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life faces fear with courage, trusts its partners, and keeps a "sound soul in a sound mind and a sound body" (the DWMA motto and the last chapter's title). Neither absolute order nor madness is the answer; courage and human bonds are.

delivery.evidence: No review found calls it preachy; a MyAnimeList reviewer calls Medusa "one-dimensional" while praising Stein.
delivery.note: Its message about courage over fear is stated in key lines (ch. 60, 112, 113) but mostly carried by fights and gags.

personified.ideology: Fear and madness; order is arbitrary

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (courage), Pagan / occult (as setting), Communitarianism, Existentialism, Secular humanism.

entry.heading: Grand Blue Dreaming
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is lived with loyal friends who laugh together, push each other past their comfort zones and share the sea; youth is for fun, and embarrassment fades.

content.framing: Endorsed (played for laughs); occasional comic consequences

delivery.evidence: ScreenWise: refusing a drink is "portrayed as a social failure"; Anime Feminist: humor relies on coercion. No review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its message about friendship and letting loose comes through running gags, not stated lessons; the sober view is held by characters who are often the butt of jokes.

personified.ideology: Hedonism and brotherhood through shared excess
Reluctant conformist who learns to enjoy the group

entry.dominant: Hedonism, Communitarianism, Expressive individualism.

entry.heading: Record of Ragnarok
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is a defiant one: human beings prove their worth by refusing to bow, fighting to the end for the people they love, and earning respect even from those who would destroy them.

delivery.evidence: TV Tropes calls the gods "Jerkass Gods," though Heracles, Buddha and Shiva get nuance; sabukaru sees "no blasphemy or ill-intent." No review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The theme of human worth is stated in speeches and commentary, while the gods' side is mostly arrogance with a few respected exceptions.

personified.ideology: Defiance of divine authority; human worth
Divine right to judge and end humanity
Protective love of humanity without hatred

entry.dominant: Secular humanism (as human worth against the gods), Might makes right (as the tournament's format), Classical virtue ethics, Pagan/occult (polytheistic setting), Existentialism.

entry.heading: Gachiakuta
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: Nothing and no one is trash. Things and people that others throw away hold value, and a good life repairs, cherishes and protects them instead of discarding them.

delivery.evidence: Bleeding Cool: elites "comically, sneeringly evil"; Otaku Orbit: "rich people are bad, poor people are oppressed"; A.V. Club: "persistent undercurrents of class disparity."
delivery.note: The anti-waste and anti-caste message is stated openly through Rudo and Regto, while the wealthy are drawn broadly and the Raiders' violent answer gets more nuance.

personified.ideology: Dignity of the discarded; anger at caste injustice
Hereditary caste and contempt for the poor
Care and repair of what others throw away

entry.dominant: Critical theory, Communitarianism, Environmentalism, Secular humanism, Pagan/occult (animism).

entry.heading: The Way of the Househusband
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is a quiet, devoted one: you can leave a violent past behind, and caring for your home and spouse deserves the same skill, pride and seriousness as any job.

delivery.evidence: Feminism in India says fears it would be "too preachy" do not hold up; reviewers praise deadpan gags, not lessons.
delivery.note: Its message about peace and the dignity of housework comes through repeated gag contrasts; the opposing view (that Tatsu must return to crime) is held by sympathetic foils who are always shown wrong.

personified.ideology: Peaceful domestic devotion; masculine intensity redirected to care
Yakuza loyalty; the boss belongs in the gang
Career woman with a supportive househusband
Judging a man by his past and looks

entry.dominant: Communitarianism, Classical virtue ethics, Progressivism (gender roles), Traditionalism (marriage and domestic craft).

entry.heading: Claymore
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life holds onto its humanity under pressure. You stay loyal to comrades and to the dead, refuse to be used as someone else's weapon, and choose solidarity with other outcasts over power or revenge.

content.framing: Mixed: some shown as threat or horror, some fan service

delivery.evidence: ANN (Martin): "ultimately more a human story than anything else." No review in the entry calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its themes of humanity and institutional exploitation emerge through plot reveals and characters' choices rather than speeches.

personified.ideology: Loyalty and humanity kept despite a monstrous body
People as weapons; ends justify means
Faith community moving from exclusion to hospitality
Power without restraint, born of trauma

entry.dominant: Communitarianism, Existentialism, Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued), Transhumanism (critiqued), Feminism (explored).

entry.heading: Blood on the Tracks
entry.label: From summaries

delivery.evidence: The Beat says it avoids demonizing, treating mother and son as products of a failing family; Oshimi avoided "an obvious monster parent."
delivery.note: The series shows the abuse entirely through the son's perception and lets consequences and the mother's revealed past, not statements, carry its judgments.

personified.ideology: Escape through outside love and honesty

entry.dominant: Existentialism (the self that must be claimed), a Dharmic echo of attachment and inherited harm, and Confucian filial duty explored under strain; Nihilism voiced in the adult arc and moved past.

entry.heading: Bloom Into You
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is lived as your true self, not as the person others expect, and real love lets the other person change and grow rather than freezing them in place.

delivery.evidence: Friedman calls it "intriguing, rather than entertaining"; Bauman calls it "not as original as we like to think." No reviewer found calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Views on masks, romance and its absence get fair voices, but no character in the main manga voices a traditional objection to same-sex love.

entry.dominant: Expressive individualism, Existentialism, Progressivism, Secular humanism.

entry.heading: BLAME!
entry.label: From summaries

delivery.evidence: Story told "mostly... with his art, and only spartan amounts of dialog" (SelfAwarePatterns); "mystery without explanation can become the entire point" (Yokogao).
delivery.note: The near-wordless storytelling leaves almost every idea implicit, so readers supply most of the meaning themselves.

personified.ideology: Silent persistence on behalf of humanity

entry.dominant: Transhumanism (explored, not endorsed), Existentialism, Nihilism and Absurdism (as mood), Naturalism.

entry.heading: Call of the Night (Yofukashi no Uta)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is one you choose for yourself. Freedom, honesty about your feelings and real connection matter more than fitting in, and love means staying with someone even when it costs you.

delivery.evidence: ANN's This Week in Anime says the show "makes a pseudo-moral argument in favor of truancy"; reviewers otherwise praise its quiet, introspective tone.
delivery.note: Its case for freedom and honest feeling comes through mood and character arcs rather than speeches, while school and parents are mostly absent rather than argued against.

personified.ideology: Freedom and self-discovery outside school norms

entry.dominant: Expressive individualism, Existentialism, Hedonism (explored, then tempered).

entry.heading: Fire Force
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is the hero's life: you keep hope against despair, protect people even when they call you a devil, and treat your team as a family. Faith is honored when it is sincere and serves people; institutions that use faith to control people are exposed.

content.framing: Neutral to Endorsed (as comedy); questioned in ch. 280

delivery.evidence: Drunken Anime Blog finds the church "at times good and at times bad"; TV Tropes calls Hibana's atheism a straw portrayal.
delivery.note: The series lets sincere believers, skeptics and fanatics each speak, but the church's leadership and its fanatic priest are drawn as plain villains.

personified.ideology: Hope and heroism; faith has worth whatever its object

entry.dominant: Communitarianism, Classical virtue ethics, Nihilism (critiqued), Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued), Pantheist/New Age.

entry.heading: Look Back
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is spent making things with and for other people. Talent and rivalry are not enough; art is worth the grind because of who it is shared with. Loss cannot be undone, but it can be carried forward into work.

delivery.evidence: Polygon praised its subtlety (via Wikipedia); ANN calls the wordless final scene affecting; no reviewer found calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The message is carried by images and silence, and Fujino's despair ("I hate drawing") gets a fair hearing before the ending answers it.

personified.ideology: Art as ambition, then art for another
Art as devotion and a way out of isolation

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Secular humanism, Classical virtue ethics, Stoicism.

series.title: Wotakoi: Love is Hard for Otaku

entry.heading: Wotakoi: Love Is Hard for Otaku (Fujita)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is shared with people who accept the whole of you, hobbies included; you need not hide what you love, and those who love you should let you open up at your own pace.

content.framing: Neutral to Endorsed (social drinking as normal adult life); occasional comic consequences

delivery.evidence: Fujita rates the mix "comedy 8, romance 1.5, seriousness 0.5" (Anime Corner); critics call it breezy and genuine.
delivery.note: Its anti-stigma theme emerges through gags and small arcs, and the non-otaku Naoya is drawn as kindly as the otaku.

personified.ideology: Hiding one's hobbies to fit social norms
Guarding a respectable image while secretly a fan

entry.dominant: Expressive individualism, Communitarianism, Consumerism, Secular humanism.

entry.heading: Yotsuba&!
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is lived with open eyes in ordinary days: curiosity, play, honesty and the kindness of family, friends and neighbors make each day worth enjoying. Family is made by love and care, not only by blood.

delivery.evidence: Santos (ANN): "sincere storytelling" evoking "the sweet, simple joys of childhood"; Tennekoon (Solrad): "never saccharine." No source calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The series shows its values through everyday episodes and almost never states them, and no character argues for an opposing worldview.

personified.ideology: Wonder and enjoying each ordinary day
Family made by love and present, hands-on fatherhood

entry.dominant: Communitarianism, Classical virtue ethics, Confucian ethics, Dharmic (Buddhist mindfulness), Traditionalism. All are mild; the series argues for nothing loudly.

entry.heading: Ajin: Demi-Human
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life holds on to particular human bonds and keeps trying to do right in a cruel world, even when cold calculation says to walk away. Treating people (or immortals) as tools, whether by a state lab or a terrorist, is shown as monstrous.

content.framing: Shown with consequences; terror and torture condemned
Neutral (as a game mechanic) and shown with consequences (trauma)

delivery.evidence: Reviewers praise "complex morally gray protagonists" (Diabolical Plots) and Evil Versus Evil framing (TV Tropes); no review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Kei states his utilitarian logic aloud (ch. 43) and Nakano answers him, but most themes come through plot and tactics rather than speeches.

personified.ideology: Life as a game; terrorism as liberation
Empathy and moral duty to strangers
State utilitarianism for the greater good

entry.dominant: Utilitarianism, Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued), Might makes right (critiqued), Critical theory, Secular humanism.

series.title: JoJo’s Bizarre Adventure: Part 8—JoJolion
series.romaji: JoJo no Kimyou na Bouken: JoJolion
series.native: ジョジョの奇妙な冒険 ジョジョリオン

entry.heading: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure Part 8: JoJolion
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is found in the people who choose you: identity is built from love, debt and loyalty, not only from blood or memory; healing has a price, and greed for a shortcut destroys families, while sacrifice for others breaks curses.

delivery.evidence: CBR calls the final villain "an enigma"; a student review says "the villain sucks"; Araki calls JoJo "an ode to humanity."
delivery.note: Themes of curse, identity and the cost of healing come through plot and imagery, while the villains' views are stated briefly and left thin.

personified.ideology: Identity made from bonds and debts, not memory or blood
The strong survive, the weak are destroyed; family pride
Rock Human supremacy; calamity without right or wrong

entry.dominant: Existentialism (identity, affirmed), Communitarianism (found family, affirmed), Classical virtue ethics (affirmed), Confucian ethics (explored through inherited sin and filial duty), with Might makes right, Utilitarianism and Consumerism critiqued.

entry.heading: Noragami: Stray God
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is one you choose, not one you were made for: you can turn from a violent past, take responsibility for the people bound to you, and keep faith with the ties (en) that make you real to others.

delivery.evidence: Kotaku praises its arcs about letting go of the past; no review opened calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its message about choosing who you become is carried by plot and character arcs, with comedy keeping speeches short.

personified.ideology: Redemption by choice, not by origin
A maker owns and uses what he makes
Control the dangerous for the common good

entry.dominant: Pagan/occult (Shinto folk), Existentialism, Classical virtue ethics, Communitarianism, Dharmic.

series.title: That Time I Got Reincarnated as a Slime
series.native: 転生したらスライムだった件

entry.heading: That Time I Got Reincarnated as a Slime
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is building a home where very different people can live together in peace, through friendship, hard work and fair dealing, protected by a ruler strong enough to deter anyone who would destroy it.

content.frequency: Frequent in the war arcs; low in nation-building stretches
content.framing: Shown with consequences (attack on Tempest); largely endorsed (Rimuru's retaliation)

delivery.evidence: ANN's Eisenbeis says the show asks viewers to side with Rimuru and fails; TV Tropes notes a "Strawman Has a Point" reading of Falmuth.
delivery.note: Its ideals of coexistence and benevolent rule are shown through Rimuru's choices and his followers' praise more than through speeches.

personified.ideology: Benevolent rule backed by overwhelming power

personified.character: King Edmaris and the Falmuth army
personified.ideology: Human supremacy and fear of monsters
Nihilism: destroy the world to remake it

lenses.label: Might makes right
lenses.stance: Explored (rejected as a creed by villains, practiced by the hero)

entry.dominant: Collectivism/authoritarianism, Communitarianism, Pragmatism, Utilitarianism, Might makes right.

entry.heading: Rent-A-Girlfriend (Reiji Miyajima)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life means loving someone sincerely and showing up for them, even when the relationship started as a paid act. Lies told for others can hide a truth, but they have to be faced in the end.

content.framing: Neutral to played for comedy (fan service and Kazuya's lust); Explored (paid intimacy)
Mixed: deception is sustained and partly excused, then exposed

content.frequency: Pervasive (premise) and recurring outside the book

delivery.evidence: Reviewers debate whether it critiques or indulges Kazuya; Aftermath calls it "narrative purgatory"; Anime Feminist says Chizuru is "treated with due respect."
delivery.note: Its ideas about loneliness, paid intimacy and honesty come through situation comedy and long arcs, and the story rarely states a verdict outright.

personified.ideology: Sincere devotion as the answer to loneliness
Pursue your dream; lies that protect a truth

lenses.label: Feminism
lenses.stance: Explored (by critics and the ch. 380 debate)

entry.dominant: Consumerism, Expressive individualism, Pragmatism.

entry.heading: Ao Haru Ride (Blue Spring Ride)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life means being honest about who you are and what you feel, even when it costs you friends or safety. Grief and fear of loss must be faced, not hidden, and real friends are the ones who see you clearly.

content.framing: Shown with consequences (healed through honesty and connection)

delivery.evidence: Reviewers praise realism; Hopper (ANN) calls its high school personas "spot on." No review opened calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its message about honesty is spoken in Futaba's narration and confrontations but mostly shown through slow character change.

personified.ideology: Self-protection by closing off from love

entry.dominant: Expressive individualism, Classical virtue ethics, Communitarianism, Secular humanism.

entry.heading: Mashle: Magic and Muscles
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is a quiet one: protect your family, be kind, work hard, enjoy simple pleasures (cream puffs), and judge people by what they do, not by the gifts they were born with.

content.framing: Neutral (mostly slapstick); shown with consequences in late arcs

delivery.evidence: Reason calls it absurdist comedy with a point about discrimination; Anime Feminist calls the villain cop cartoonishly corrupt. No review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The anti-discrimination message rides under deadpan gags, with early villains cartoonish and later opponents given reasons and redemption.

personified.ideology: The strong may take from the weak
Law and order; the magicless as a threat

entry.dominant: Libertarianism (anti-state-discrimination reading), Classical virtue ethics, Critical theory (caste satire), Secular humanism, Communitarianism.

entry.heading: Nana
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is found in honest, loyal bonds with the people you choose, more than in romance, fame or getting what you want; the story shows that running from loneliness through sex, drugs or dependence on another person costs a great deal, and it does not say whether a happy ending is possible.

delivery.evidence: The Mary Sue: "very realistic, with little room for romantic tropes"; Web Japan: "about the realities of life." No reviewer found calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The series shows the results of its characters' choices through events and inner narration rather than stating morals, and it leaves most judgments to the reader.

personified.ideology: Romantic dependence and the wish for an ordinary home

entry.dominant: Expressive individualism, Existentialism, Feminism, Secular humanism, Dharmic (Buddhist, by echo).

series.title: Boy's Abyss
series.adult_reason: Boy's Abyss: VIZ rates it Mature; Publishers Weekly notes explicit sex, incl. a minor with adults; deep entry scores 9

entry.heading: Boy's Abyss
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: The series presents a good life as one where a young person breaks free of the adults and the town that use him, faces the truth about his family and chooses to keep living on his own terms. VIZ's blurb puts the problem plainly: "Self-serving adults and broken dreams push a teenager toward the abyss."

content.framing: Mixed: abuse shown as harm and punished, but often drawn as charged romance
Shown with consequences, with a romanticized legend

delivery.evidence: VIZ's blurb blames "self-serving adults"; ANN says it does not glorify suicide; CBR calls the suicide legend's framing "incredibly controversial."
delivery.note: The story shows its verdict through consequences rather than speeches, but its abusers are drawn with allure as well as blame.

personified.ideology: Possessive protection that excuses abuse of power
Family duty as a hold over a child
Art that uses real people as material

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Nihilism (explored and critiqued), Expressive individualism (escape from family), Critical theory (power of adults over the young).

entry.heading: Made in Abyss
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life follows its longing into the unknown, whatever the cost. Wonder, curiosity and love are worth suffering and even death; the world itself is indifferent, and value is something people choose and pay for.

content.framing: Neutral (often played as comedy); criticized by reviewers

delivery.evidence: No review opened calls it preachy; ANN notes Bondrewd "sees himself as doing good"; Beneath the Tangles says the mercy killing takes no side.
delivery.note: The series shows rather than argues, leaving euthanasia, experimentation and the worth of longing as open questions.

personified.ideology: Longing and curiosity worth any cost
Progress and knowledge justify using children
Vengeance as love for a mother

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Expressive individualism, Naturalism; Utilitarianism and Transhumanism are critiqued through Bondrewd.

entry.heading: Pandora Hearts
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: Your existence is not a sin. A good life means accepting who you are, facing the truth about the past instead of trying to undo it, and choosing to keep going for the people you love, even when your origin is a lie.

delivery.evidence: No reviewer found calls it preachy. Morrissy (ANN) praises factions that shift "between friend and enemy" and twists that make sense in hindsight.
delivery.note: The message about self-worth emerges through mystery reveals and Oz's choices more than speeches, though key lines state it outright late in the series.

personified.ideology: Self-acceptance: existence is not a sin
Duty to the world above personal love
Religion as fraud promising paradise in the Abyss

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Pagan/occult (fantasy), Secular humanism, Expressive individualism, Dharmic (rebirth and attachment).

entry.heading: Fairy Tail
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is lived among friends who become family. You belong to a group that accepts you as you are, you protect its members at any cost, you forgive former enemies who join you, and you get stronger for the sake of others.

content.framing: Played for laughs (fan service); Condemned (forced stripping)

delivery.evidence: CBR says villains fall "with the power of friendship"; Burnett: "this gets said and shown a lot." Silverman (ANN): "cheesy," but the show pulls it off.
delivery.note: The friendship theme is spoken aloud in battle speeches and confirmed by plot wins, while most villains are either redeemed or left thinly motivated.

personified.ideology: Friends as the source of strength
Strength alone has value; discard the weak
Despair and the curse of endless life

entry.dominant: Communitarianism, Classical virtue ethics, Expressive individualism, Pagan/occult (as fantasy setting), Secular humanism.

entry.heading: Nisekoi: False Love (Naoshi Komi)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: Love is proven by who you become together, not by fate or by a past promise; kindness, honesty about your feelings and loyalty to friends make a good life.

content.framing: Endorsed (romance, ending in marriage); Neutral (fan-service gags)

delivery.evidence: Reviewers call it cliché, light comedy ("packed to the rafters with clichés," UK Anime Network); none call it preachy.
delivery.note: Its view of love emerges through running gags and the final choice, while the gang setting and harem conventions go unexamined.

personified.ideology: Love chosen in the present over a destined promise

entry.dominant: Expressive individualism, Traditionalism, Communitarianism.

entry.heading: Delicious in Dungeon
entry.label: From summaries

delivery.evidence: Reviewers praise its "debates about where to draw the line" on eating (SLJ); Geeks Under Grace notes no moralizing. No review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its ideas about eating, mortality and prejudice come through arguments between characters and the plot rather than lectures.

personified.ideology: Eat what you kill, waste nothing, respect the ecosystem
Love that refuses death; overcoming mortality
Short-lived races first; distrust of power
Possessive loyalty, preserving a kingdom by force

entry.dominant: Environmentalism (ecology), Pragmatism, Communitarianism, Secular humanism, Classical virtue ethics.

entry.heading: GTO: Great Teacher Onizuka
entry.label: From summaries

content.framing: Mixed: often comic and endorsed when Onizuka does it; shown with consequences for villains
Played for comedy; abuse shown with consequences

delivery.evidence: Kimlinger (ANN): works "as both a parody and as the thing it parodies"; Thompson: "approaches true social satire." No review found calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Lessons arrive through Onizuka's speeches at climaxes and through rescues, inside broad comedy that also mocks the uplifting-teacher genre.

personified.ideology: School as a business, surveillance and metrics

entry.dominant: Pragmatism, Classical virtue ethics, Communitarianism, Libertarianism (anti-institutional), Critical theory (of schooling).

entry.heading: Blue Box
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is lived by trying with everything you have, at your sport and in love, so you will not regret it. Honesty with others, and patience in love, matter more than winning.

delivery.evidence: Reviewers praise restraint: "never becomes tacky or prurient" (ANN); "doesn't abuse the shoujo romantic tropes" (SLJ). None call it preachy.
delivery.note: Its messages about effort and honesty come through Taiki's narration and the parallel sports and romance plots rather than speeches.

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Existentialism (striving without regret), Communitarianism (team and host family), Expressive individualism (following one's feelings).

series.title: Chained Soldier
series.adult_reason: Chained Soldier: Yen Press rates it 18+ M (Mature); built-in sexual 'reward' scenes, nudity; deep entry scores sexuality 8

entry.heading: Chained Soldier (Mato Seihei no Slave)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is lived in service to your team and the people you love: be diligent, loyal and brave, protect the weak, and keep your promises. Physical pleasure is shown as a fair and fun payoff for hard work.

delivery.evidence: Reviews say the gender-politics premise is raised then underused (MyAnimeList review; Anime Feminist); none call it preachy.
delivery.note: Its values come through Yuuki's conduct and the reward mechanic rather than stated lessons, and its gender-reversed society is mostly backdrop.

personified.ideology: Duty and command fueled by revenge

entry.dominant: Hedonism, Communitarianism, Classical virtue ethics, Might makes right (as the power system), Pagan / occult (Japanese myth).

entry.heading: ReLIFE
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is not lost when you fall out of society. You can restart it by facing your past honestly, letting others in, and helping the people beside you, even when it hurts.

delivery.evidence: ANN says flashbacks show lessons Arata applies; no review opened calls it preachy. Black company shown only as harmful.
delivery.note: The message comes through Kaizaki's flashbacks and his advice to classmates rather than speeches, though the workplace side has no sympathetic voice.

personified.ideology: Restart is possible; honesty and connection heal
Quiet support and second chances, within company rules
Efficiency over cooperation, then learning connection

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Communitarianism, Secular humanism, Existentialism, Critical theory (labor).

entry.heading: The Seven Deadly Sins
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is lived in loyal love and friendship, chosen across the lines that clans, races and gods draw. Love and loyalty should outlast curses, prejudice and even the rulers of heaven and hell.

content.framing: Endorsed (played as comedy); critics call it harassment

delivery.evidence: Otaku USA says the series "humanizes its villains"; the Demon King and Supreme Deity get little inner life. No review found calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its themes of love across clan lines and forgiveness come through backstory flashbacks and battle speeches rather than lectures.

personified.ideology: Love defies clan law and divine curse
Rule by fear and clan hatred
Order by force; war to save the kingdom

entry.dominant: Communitarianism (found family), Expressive individualism (love against clan law), Pagan / occult (Celtic fantasy), Traditionalism, Classical virtue ethics.

entry.heading: Solanin
entry.label: From summaries

delivery.evidence: The Fandom Post: Asano "doesn't offer easy solutions"; ComicsAlliance notes the record executive's sell-out choice gets a fair justification.
delivery.note: The story weighs dream against stability through characters and leaves the verdict largely to the reader.

personified.ideology: Pursuing the dream of music over "proper work"
Practical stability; happiness need not be the hard road
Pride set aside for a career inside the industry

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Secular humanism, Pragmatism, Dharmic (Buddhist) by echo, Expressive individualism (explored).

entry.heading: Assassination Classroom
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life comes from finding your own strength, being seen and believed in by someone, and facing hard things together. Nobody is worthless because a system ranks them low, and anyone, even a killer, can change.

content.frequency: Constant (as premise); bloody only in a few arcs

delivery.evidence: Matsui calls it "lessons upon lessons"; one MyAnimeList review faults "superficial satire". No review in this entry calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Koro-sensei states each lesson aloud, while the opposing view (Asano's fear-based system) gets a sympathetic backstory but Takaoka is drawn as a plain sadist.

personified.ideology: Personal, caring education; redemption through service

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Secular humanism, Communitarianism, Confucian ethics.

entry.heading: Yona of the Dawn
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is one where privilege is turned into service: you face hard truths, grow strong enough to protect others, keep faith with the people who stand by you, and refuse revenge in favor of healing the land.

delivery.evidence: ANN praises the "political complexity"; Anime Feminist hosts praise villains as "complex individuals who aren't entirely evil." No review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its messages about just rule and service are spoken in Yona's lines and shown through the villages she helps, while Su-won's opposing view gets a fair hearing.

personified.ideology: Rule as service to the people
Greed and exploitation of the weak

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Confucian ethics, Communitarianism, Feminism.

entry.heading: Dragon Ball (manga, 1984-1995)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is one of joyful striving: train hard, keep getting stronger, enjoy the fight, protect your friends, forgive rivals and give former enemies a place at the table.

content.frequency: Constant in the second half; frequent in the first
content.framing: Endorsed (fighting as virtue), with deaths shown with consequences
Played for laughs; Roshi's lechery is mocked but rarely punished

delivery.evidence: Inferred from the entry's summaries; no review addresses preachiness.
delivery.note: Values of effort and friendship come through comedy and fights with little direct moral commentary.

lenses.label: Might makes right
lenses.stance: Explored (critiqued in villains, affirmed in plot mechanics)

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Might makes right (critiqued in villains, affirmed in plot mechanics), Dharmic (Hindu/Buddhist) cosmology, Pagan/occult-style folk polytheism (as setting), Pragmatism.

series.title: The Guy She Was Interested In Wasn't a Guy at All
series.romaji: Ki ni Natteru Hito ga Otoko ja Nakatta
series.native: 気になってる人が男じゃなかった

entry.heading: The Guy She Was Interested In Wasn't a Guy at All
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is lived openly as yourself, among people who share what you love; music is how you find them, and real friends and partners back each other's dreams.

delivery.evidence: Nippon.com says the same-sex relationship is treated as unremarkable; no reviewer found calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The mocking classmate Narita is redeemed fairly, but no character voices a traditional objection to same-sex love or to Mitsuki's dress.

personified.ideology: Owning your tastes over social conformity
Mockery of the odd one out, later loyalty

entry.dominant: Expressive individualism, Communitarianism, Progressivism.

entry.title: Pluto
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
