entry.life_message: A good life means choosing to stop the cycle of hatred, even when you have reason to hate.

content.note: Serial murders of robots and humans; war backstory (Wikipedia; AniList War 77%, Noir).
Dark murder mystery; Urasawa calls Tezuka's source 'very dark' (Wikipedia); AniList Psychological, Tragedy.
Grief and war trauma; AniList Suicide signal (specifics to verify).

entry.dominant: Secular humanism, Transhumanism

delivery.evidence: Jason Thompson (ANN) calls its Iraq War political content heavy-handed and the parallels shallow; ANN's Santos praises its philosophical points

personified.ideology: refusing hatred despite reason to hate

delivery.note: Its anti-hatred, anti-war message runs through an obvious Iraq War allegory that one critic finds heavy-handed.

series.title: Deadman Wonderland
series.native: デッドマン・ワンダーランド

entry.heading: Deadman Wonderland
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is one you choose to keep living after injustice and loss. You hold on to friends, refuse to become the monster that hurt you, and show mercy instead of taking revenge. People who treat others as entertainment, property or lab material are the real criminals.

content.framing: Condemned (as cruelty for profit and pleasure); shown with consequences
Mixed: some fan service played for comedy, sexual violence condemned
Shown with consequences; suicide finally rejected

delivery.evidence: ANN's Kimlinger says it avoids "ponderous moralizing," with only "the occasional swipe at dehumanizing prison conditions and privatized punishment."
delivery.note: Its critique of punishment as spectacle is built into the setting and the crowd scenes; most villains are open sadists, and several get sympathetic backstories.

personified.ideology: Will to live and mercy over revenge
Profit and pleasure from others' suffering
Despair and a wish to die

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Critical theory (critique of the prison system), Secular humanism, Communitarianism.

series.title: Golden Kamuy
series.adult_reason: Golden Kamuy: VIZ rates it Mature (18+, VIZ Signature); extreme gore, cannibalism, human-skin horror, crude sexual gags; deep entry scores 9

entry.heading: Golden Kamuy
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is lived by your own hands and promises: survive with skill, respect the animals and land that feed you, keep faith with the dead and the living, and refuse to let greed or other men's wars decide your future.

delivery.evidence: Reviewers praise its morally gray factions (MAL, ANN); Rika Ito argues it offers a "sanitized Ainu-Japanese relationship"; Anime Feminist flags a "problematically written trans woman."
delivery.note: The story lets nationalist, separatist and Indigenous causes speak through likable characters, but critics question how it handles colonial history and one trans character.

personified.ideology: Ainu tradition renewed by a new generation

entry.dominant: Pragmatism (survival), Pagan / animist (Ainu), Classical virtue ethics, Environmentalism, Communitarianism.

entry.heading: To Your Eternity (Fumetsu no Anata e)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is made of the people you love and who change you. Pain and loss are the price of connection and the way a person grows. A life without end is only worth living if it is shared, and even the immortal must let others go.

delivery.evidence: ANN's Beckett finds the Church "so comically evil" and Hayase's motives not "well-communicated"; no review calls the series preachy.
delivery.note: Its messages about grief and connection are shown through deaths and Fushi's reactions, with the Beholder and others sometimes stating them aloud.

personified.ideology: Humanity learned through love and loss

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Dharmic (Hindu/Buddhist), Secular humanism, Classical virtue ethics, Communitarianism.

entry.heading: Girls' Last Tour
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is found in companionship, curiosity and small joys, even when there is no future to build. Memory and record-keeping matter, but letting go matters too.

delivery.evidence: TCJ: "it does not moralize" beyond "implicit dismay towards war." One MyAnimeList review called the existential tone heavy-handed.
delivery.note: Ideas come through quiet dialogue between Chito and Yuuri, who are given equal weight, and the story rarely states a conclusion.

personified.ideology: Memory and knowledge give life meaning
Live in the present; enjoy what is here
A life's purpose in one project

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Dharmic (Buddhist impermanence), Absurdism, Secular humanism.

entry.heading: Real
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life means facing your real situation, not the one you had or the one others rank you by. It takes daily effort and honest connection with others, and your worth does not depend on your body, your status or your wins.

delivery.evidence: Reviewers say it resists easy inspiration: "unforgiving, much like life" (Manga Bookshelf); leads "flawed and believable rather than saintly."
delivery.note: Its lessons come through setbacks and character change rather than speeches, though Anime Feminist finds some disability stereotypes.

personified.ideology: Human worth measured by rank and ability

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Classical virtue ethics, Secular humanism, Stoicism, Communitarianism.

entry.heading: Choujin X
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life means finding your own will instead of living in someone else's shadow, and using whatever you become to protect others. Power drawn from desire is dangerous; it is redeemed by empathy, friendship and honesty about yourself.

delivery.evidence: Reviews praise sympathetic villains (Batista "a great tragic villain"); TV Tropes calls Queem a "Complete Monster". No review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its ideas about identity and desire are built into the power system and the villains' backstories rather than spoken as lessons.

personified.ideology: Rewrite the past for the greater good

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Expressive individualism, Classical virtue ethics, Transhumanism (explored).

series.title: Onani Master Kurosawa
series.native: オナニーマスター黒沢
series.adult_reason: Onani Master Kurosawa: explicit at its core (premise centers on a junior-high protagonist's masturbation); MangaUpdates genre Mature, tag Masturbation; ANN content 'Intense'; English edition from Denpa (MangaUpdates also lists Fakku), publisher age rating unconfirmed
series.warning: The premise centers on a junior-high student's masturbation; sexual content involves minors.

entry.title: Onani Master Kurosawa
entry.label: Quick read (from summaries)
entry.life_message: It holds up facing one's wrongdoing, opening up to others and changing, rather than hiding in contempt and isolation.

content.note: Mostly school conflict; little physical violence reported (to verify).
Psychological tension, guilt and humiliation rather than horror.
Masturbation is the premise; sexual harassment of classmates and rape fantasies (ANN, MAL reviews, AniList tags); reviewers say not visually explicit.
Bullying, isolation, blackmail and self-loathing drive the plot (ANN, MangaUpdates, MAL reviews).
Soiling classmates' belongings as revenge and harassment; reviewers split on whether consequences are adequate.

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Hedonism (critiqued), Classical virtue ethics

delivery.evidence: No source addresses delivery; redemption theme carried by Kurosawa's guilt and change (to verify).
delivery.note: Kurosawa's turn from contempt to remorse carries the message, while the harmed girls receive less attention.

understated: Fear and intensity: database tags (Tragedy) suggest more than 2/10

entry.heading: Magi: The Labyrinth of Magic
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is chosen freely rather than handed down by fate or by a ruler. You face your own pain without sinking into hatred, treat every people as equal, and work with friends to build a world without slaves or masters, even if a free world stays messy and cruel.

delivery.evidence: TV Tropes calls Magnostadt's grievances "partly justified"; fans split on Sinbad. No review in the entry calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Themes of fate, kingship and equality are argued in long speeches and shown through rulers whose plans are given a real hearing before they fail.

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Secular humanism, Classical virtue ethics, Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued), Critical theory, Communitarianism.

entry.heading: Boruto: Naruto Next Generations (Ukyo Kodachi, Masashi Kishimoto and Mikio Ikemoto, 2016-)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is one where you protect the people you love, carry your parents' legacy without being trapped by it, and keep your own sense of who you are even when everyone else sees you wrongly.

delivery.evidence: TV Tropes lists the "Talk-no-Jutsu return" as a fan dispute; ANN praises its generational theme. No review found calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its points about fathers, legacy and identity come through the plot's twists more than speeches, though rival views are argued mid-fight.

personified.ideology: Honor your legacy but forge your own path
Protect loved ones by any means, even control
Higher beings may harvest lesser ones
Duty to all before time with family

entry.dominant: Communitarianism (family and village), Classical virtue ethics, Transhumanism (critiqued), Confucian ethics. Lens labels are this entry's own framing unless a source is named.

entry.heading: Mob Psycho 100
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is not defined by talent or power. You become a good person by how you treat others, by honest effort and by accepting all of yourself, including the feelings you would rather hide.

content.framing: Condemned (as a way to solve problems); shown with consequences

delivery.evidence: /Film: Mob "peel[s] away the villain's layers of self loathing"; villains get backstories. No review in this entry calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Lessons are stated outright in Reigen's and Mob's speeches, while villains' worldviews are given real backstories and are argued with, not mocked.

personified.ideology: Worth comes from kindness and effort, not power
Street-smart pragmatism; self-interest softened by care
Misanthropy: people are wicked at heart

lenses.label: Confucian ethics, Traditionalism, Progressivism, Utilitarianism, Postmodernism, Absurdism, Hedonism

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Secular humanism, Pragmatism, Existentialism, with Might makes right and Collectivism / authoritarianism clearly critiqued.

entry.heading: BEASTARS
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life means knowing your own nature, including its dangerous urges, and choosing to master them for the sake of others, while refusing the labels a society hands you. Love and coexistence across a deep divide are possible, but only with honesty, restraint and a cost.

content.framing: Neutral to sympathetic (Haru); shown with consequences (predation as desire)

delivery.evidence: MAL reviewer Krunchyman says Itagaki "never pointed the finger"; another (qwyxivi) feels it was made "mostly for the sake of social commentary."
delivery.note: The prejudice and appetite themes are carried by the premise and characters' inner monologues more than by speeches, and villains get sympathetic backstories.

personified.ideology: Herbivore pride and will to power
Predation as true love; instinct as the real self

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Classical virtue ethics, Naturalism, Secular humanism, Critical theory.

entry.heading: Akame ga KILL!
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is spent fighting for the weak against a cruel order, even at the cost of your own life and innocence. Killing the wicked is shown as necessary, but never as clean: the killers call it murder and expect to pay for it.

content.framing: Shown with consequences (heroes' killings); Condemned (villains' torture)
Condemned (sexual violence, shown as villains' crimes); Neutral (fan service)

delivery.evidence: ANN (vol. 1) praises "shades of gray"; MAL reviewer calls villains "almost comically evil"; Sportskeeda: anime "became too black and white."
delivery.note: The anti-tyranny message is carried by action and backstories; the Empire's side gets sympathetic Jaegers but cartoonish top villains.

personified.ideology: Social Darwinism, strength as the only law
Corrupt power for its own pleasure
Loyal service to a state he believes is good

entry.dominant: Might makes right (critiqued), Collectivism / authoritarianism (critiqued), Utilitarianism, Pragmatism, Classical virtue ethics.

series.title: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure Part 1: Phantom Blood
series.romaji: JoJo no Kimyou na Bouken: Phantom Blood
series.native: ジョジョの奇妙な冒険 ファントムブラッド

entry.heading: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure Part 1: Phantom Blood
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is lived as a "gentleman": with courage that knows fear and masters it, loyalty to family and friends, and self-sacrifice for the weak. Being human, with its limits and its death, is better than power gained by giving up one's humanity.

delivery.evidence: Araki calls Jonathan and Dio "good and evil, white and black"; Zeppeli states the moral aloud ("A hymn to humanity is a hymn to courage!").
delivery.note: The moral is spoken directly by heroes and mentors, while the villain gets a real backstory and charisma but no argument the story takes seriously.

personified.ideology: Ambition and domination; transcend humanity by any means
Courage as mastering fear; humanity worth praising

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (affirmed), Traditionalism (affirmed), Secular humanism (affirmed, per Araki), Might makes right and Transhumanism (critiqued through Dio).

series.title: The Eminence in Shadow
series.native: 陰の実力者になりたくて！

entry.heading: The Eminence in Shadow
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life, as Cid lives it, is pursuing your own dream with total dedication and on your own terms, whatever others think; the story also invites readers to laugh at how self-absorbed that dream is, while his followers find meaning in loyalty and in a cause bigger than themselves.

content.frequency: Frequent; nearly every volume has killing
content.framing: Mostly Endorsed or Neutral (Cid's and Shadow Garden's killings are played as cool or comic); Condemned for the Cult

delivery.evidence: Reviewers read it as comic satire of chūnibyō power fantasies; Anime Café says it "became the anime it was trying to make fun of."
delivery.note: The story states almost no message aloud; its view emerges from the gap between Cid's narration and what really happens around him.

personified.ideology: Self-made identity; living one's fantasy whatever the cost
Loyal devotion to a leader and a cause

personified.character: The Cult of Diablos (Zenon and the Rounds)
personified.ideology: Power and immortality at others' expense

entry.dominant: Expressive individualism, Might makes right, Postmodernism (my framing), Pagan/occult.

entry.heading: Food Wars!: Shokugeki no Soma
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is spent getting better at a craft you love by cooking for real people, failing, learning from rivals and trying again. No one has the right to impose one "correct" taste on everyone else.

delivery.evidence: Dupree (ANN): Food Wars "evangelized how important a chef's personality is"; Central's members underdeveloped. No review in the entry calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The message about cooking for others and learning from failure is spoken by Soma and Joichiro and shown through duel outcomes, while the opposing elitist view gets a late sympathetic backstory but little development.

personified.ideology: Cooking for real customers; learning from failure
One enforced "True Gourmet" standard from the top
Take others' skills; win at all costs

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Expressive individualism, Hedonism, Pragmatism; Collectivism/authoritarianism as the critiqued opposite.

series.title: Mushoku Tensei: Jobless Reincarnation
series.romaji: Mushoku Tensei: Isekai Ittara Honki Dasu
series.native: 無職転生 ～異世界行ったら本気だす～
series.warning: Sources document sexual misconduct by the protagonist toward child and teen characters, often played for comedy.

entry.heading: Mushoku Tensei: Jobless Reincarnation
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is a second chance taken seriously: face the fears and shame of a wasted past, work hard, protect and rebuild your family, and keep going after failure. The story says "everybody can make mistakes" (Wikipedia's summary of the author's message), but it gives little weight to the harm its hero's sexual misconduct does to others.

content.framing: Mixed: played as comedy early; the attempted assault on Eris is rebuffed; the sex scene is framed as romance; critics say there are few consequences

delivery.evidence: Rudeus's narration states his resolve to live seriously; ScreenWise says the show "doesn't always excuse his behavior." No review found calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its message about second chances runs through Rudeus's inner monologue, while the harm he does to others is often left to comedy or quick forgiveness.

personified.ideology: Honor and protecting children against prejudice
A deity who manipulates people for his own ends

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Hedonism, Pragmatism, Classical virtue ethics, Traditionalism. (Labels are my own framing unless a source is named.)

entry.heading: The Apothecary Diaries
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is a useful one: notice what is true, learn your craft, help the people in front of you, and keep your own mind free even when your body is not. Knowledge and quiet competence protect the vulnerable better than rank, rumor or superstition.

content.frequency: Frequent (as plot), brief on the page

content.framing: Neutral to endorsed (as medicine); harmful use shown with consequences

delivery.evidence: Reviews praise nuance; Anime Feminist calls its sex-work portrayal "arguably one of the best." No opened review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its views on women's lot, reason and power come through Maomao's dry inner monologue and the outcomes of each case rather than speeches.

personified.ideology: Duty to the throne over personal desire
A survivor hardened by an abusive system

entry.dominant: Pragmatism, Naturalism (empiricism), Secular humanism, Feminism, Classical virtue ethics, Confucian ethics.

series.title: Akira
series.adult_reason: Akira: Kodansha USA rates the 2009 paperback volumes and the 2017 35th Anniversary box set 18+ (the 2025 Hardcover Collection is listed 16+); deep entry scores 9 (violence), teen drug use, sexual captivity and attempted rape involving teen characters
series.warning: Includes sexual violence involving teenage characters.

entry.heading: Akira
entry.label: From summaries

content.framing: Shown with consequences (Tetsuo's captives); Neutral (Kaneda's early behavior)

delivery.evidence: Price (ANN): "an incredibly political – and an incredibly angry – work." No review found calls it preachy or its characters strawmen.
delivery.note: The story makes its case against controlling power through plot and catastrophe rather than speeches.

personified.ideology: Youthful freedom and loyalty against all control
Power as compensation; rule by force

entry.dominant: Collectivism / authoritarianism (critiqued), Might makes right (critiqued), Transhumanism (critiqued), Existentialism, Nihilism (explored).

entry.heading: All You Need Is Kill
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is earned through effort: you fail, learn and try again until you are strong enough to protect others. Love and comradeship give the struggle meaning, but victory may cost the person you love most, and the survivor must carry that cost forward.

content.framing: Neutral (war shown as tragic but necessary)
Shown with consequences (but one suicide test is played for laughs)

delivery.evidence: No reviewer found calls it preachy; Manga Bookshelf says the manga favors "spectacle, action, and battles" over the novel's commentary.
delivery.note: The story argues for perseverance and sacrifice through events rather than speeches, but the enemy is a faceless force, so no rival worldview gets a hearing.

personified.ideology: Growth through repeated failure and effort
Discipline and care for the men under him

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Utilitarianism, Pragmatism, Existentialism.

series.title: The Girl From the Other Side: Siúil, a Rún

entry.heading: The Girl From the Other Side: Siúil, a Rún
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is gentle: you care for someone who is not your own kind, without being able to hold them, and you keep loving them whatever they turn out to be. Fear of the different, enforced by walls, purges and religious authority, destroys more than the curse it tries to stop.

delivery.evidence: ANN: "running on pure atmosphere"; Comics Beat: "much more nuanced than the premise implies." No reviewer opened calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The message is carried by images, silence and small domestic moments, and the Insiders' fear is shown as understandable even when its results are cruel.

personified.character: The church and soldiers of the Inside
personified.ideology: Safety through purge and obedience to revelation
Duty to the many versus mercy to one
Protective love that must let go

entry.dominant: Secular humanism, Dharmic (Buddhist), Critical theory (critique of exclusion), Classical virtue ethics.

series.title: Bungo Stray Dogs
series.native: 文豪ストレイドッグス

entry.heading: Bungo Stray Dogs
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is found by belonging to people who take you in, and by choosing, whatever your past, to be "on the side that saves people." No one is worthless, and an old life of killing can be left behind, but the story is also honest that the people you love can be taken from you.

content.framing: Shown with consequences (deaths of heroes); Condemned (terror attacks)
Mixed: often played for comedy; sometimes shown with consequences

delivery.evidence: Asagiri wrote villains such as Fitzgerald and Sigma to be relatable (Wikipedia); ANN calls Fyodor an "appropriately threatening" villain.
delivery.note: Themes of belonging and second chances come through backstories and action, and the main villains are given real reasons for what they do.

personified.ideology: Searching for a reason to live; from nihilism toward saving others
Humanity is sinful and must be purified
Peace through one world military power

entry.dominant: Communitarianism, Existentialism, Utilitarianism (explored), Classical virtue ethics, Nihilism (critiqued).

entry.heading: Tomo-chan Is a Girl! (Fumita Yanagida)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is being loved and accepted as you already are, by friends and by the one you love, rather than reshaping yourself to fit what a "girl" or a "guy" is supposed to be; loyal friendship is the ground that love grows from.

content.framing: Neutral (gags); shown with consequences in places

delivery.evidence: Silverman (ANN): "funny and still manages to make a point"; Kotaku: explores "how antiquated gender norms get in the way of love."
delivery.note: The gender theme comes through gags and the leads' misunderstandings, and the characters who push conformity are shown with sympathy but are proved wrong.

personified.ideology: Being loved as you are, without conforming
Girls must become feminine to be seen
Paternal authority; strength earns the right to court

entry.dominant: Expressive individualism, Classical virtue ethics, Communitarianism.

entry.heading: Mieruko-chan
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is lived with steady nerve and quiet kindness: you keep your fear to yourself, protect the people you love, honor the dead, and find out that many "monsters", living or dead, are carrying pain.

delivery.evidence: Critics praise its "restraint in explaining its monsters" and its sentimentality (Steve Jones, ANN ep. 12); no review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its themes of compassion and grief come through scene and subtext, not speeches.

personified.ideology: Spiritual craft as a paid service

entry.dominant: Pagan / occult (Japanese folk religion), Classical virtue ethics, Stoicism, Pragmatism, Dharmic (Buddhist).

series.title: Smoking Behind the Supermarket with You
series.romaji: Super no Ura de Yani Suu Futari
series.native: スーパーの裏でヤニ吸うふたり

entry.heading: Smoking Behind the Supermarket with You
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is not won by success at work. It is made bearable, and even warm, by small daily rituals, by kindness to strangers and by one person who sees who you really are when the work mask comes off.

content.framing: Endorsed (mostly); one health scare shown with consequences, then reversed

delivery.evidence: Reviewers call it low-key and "told through little scenes without words" (Tokyo Weekender); none calls it preachy; critics say it romanticizes smoking.
delivery.note: Its message about small comforts is shown through wordless routine, while the case against smoking appears mainly through a harsh boss and a health scare that is undone.

personified.ideology: Endure the grind through small comforts and decency
The true self hidden behind the work persona
Corporate authority over the worker (disapproves of smoking)

entry.dominant: Communitarianism, Hedonism (small pleasures), Expressive individualism, Existentialism. All four labels are my own framing, not a source's.

series.title: Jagaaan
series.warning: Includes the rape of a 16-year-old character and a backstory of childhood sexual abuse.

entry.heading: Jagaaan
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is not the comfortable script of job, marriage and family, nor the release of every hidden desire; it is finding out what you really want and answering for it. Desire indulged without restraint or connection turns people into monsters.

content.framing: Shown with consequences (sexual violence); otherwise neutral

delivery.evidence: No review calls it preachy; Gizmodo says the monsters' symbolism is left to readers; Anime Atelier finds no character likeable.
delivery.note: Its view of desire is shown through what each monster becomes rather than stated in speeches.

personified.ideology: Heroism as a public group project

entry.dominant: Hedonism (critiqued), Expressive individualism (critiqued), Existentialism, Dharmic (craving, this entry's framing).

entry.heading: Gokurakugai
entry.label: From summaries

delivery.evidence: MAL reviewer: issues like racism and suicide are raised but "never explored"; no review opened calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its message about chosen humanity comes through the cases and Alma's choices more than speeches, while the villains' views are sketched more than argued.

personified.ideology: Humanity is chosen by how you act
Family by blood; death as origin and return
Wanting to be human against one's nature
Weary realism that still guards a boy's humanity

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Communitarianism, Pragmatism, Dharmic (Buddhist) by imagery.

series.title: Seraph of the End: Vampire Reign

entry.heading: Seraph of the End: Vampire Reign
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is loyalty to the family you choose. You protect them, you refuse to trade any of them for a larger plan, and you stay human in a world where both rulers and rescuers use people as tools.

delivery.evidence: Kotaku says vampires are "more complex" than pure villains and the humans' actions are largely questionable; no review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its message about chosen family is stated in Yu's lines and tested through leaders who sacrifice others for larger plans.

personified.ideology: Ends justify means for those you love
Hierarchy and sacrificing the few for humanity

entry.dominant: Communitarianism (chosen family), Classical virtue ethics, Utilitarianism (critiqued), Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued), Existentialism.

entry.heading: Bakuman。 (Tsugumi Ohba and Takeshi Obata)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is a dream chased with total effort, beside a loyal partner and honest rivals, inside a demanding system you learn to master, and crowned by a promise kept. Ohba's stated message: "If you have a dream and work hard for it, I don't think it's ever a waste" (Viz interview, 2012).

content.framing: Mixed: comic or shown as wrong
Mixed: endorsed as dedication, warned against as excess

delivery.evidence: ANN's Santos finds vol. 15's lessons "somewhat heavy-handed"; TV Tropes calls the anti-pandering message "not exactly subtle."
delivery.note: Characters state the creators' views on manga and work in long dialogue; rival methods get a hearing but are judged by the Jump system's results.

personified.ideology: Dream, effort and partnership inside the editor system
Security and a safe career over dreams
A woman's ambition driven by rivalry

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Pragmatism, Expressive individualism, Traditionalism, Communitarianism.

entry.heading: The Summer Hikaru Died
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life means facing what you cannot understand without forcing it into old categories, and choosing to stay with someone who is different, even when it frightens you. A community that hides its sins and forces people into roles harms those who do not fit.

delivery.evidence: Anime Feminist: "They're showing, not telling"; ANN vol. 1: subtext "just barely shy of text." No reviewer opened calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The message rides on mood, body horror and silence, and the village's views are shown mainly through gossip rather than voiced fully.

personified.ideology: Accepting the unknown other despite fear
A monster seeking belonging and a human heart

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Pagan / occult (critiqued), Progressivism (queer identity), Critical theory (critique of conformity).

series.title: Domestic Girlfriend
series.native: ドメスティックな彼女
series.adult_reason: Domestic Girlfriend: Kodansha USA rates it 18+; sexual scenes involving high-school characters (deep entry held, sexuality 8)
series.warning: Depicts sex between characters under 18.

entry.heading: Domestic Girlfriend
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is following your heart and your calling through loss: love honestly even when society forbids it, work at the craft you were made for (writing, cooking, acting), and accept that love sometimes means sacrifice. The story lets forbidden love cost its lovers dearly, then rewards it with marriage.

content.framing: Mixed: teen sex is framed as romance; the teacher-student affair has career consequences but ends in marriage; assault is condemned

delivery.evidence: Bubbleblabber says it doesn't romanticize the teacher-student relationship; Anime Feminist says it frames abuse as forbidden love. No review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its view that sincere love justifies its costs comes through plot outcomes, not speeches, and reviewers disagree on whether it critiques or excuses the teacher-student relationship.

personified.ideology: Romantic devotion and following one's heart
Love as self-sacrifice against social rules
Independence and love that lets go

entry.dominant: Expressive individualism, Existentialism, Communitarianism, Hedonism. (Labels are my own framing unless a source is named.)

entry.heading: D.Gray-man
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is to keep walking forward through grief without trying to undo death, to love both friend and enemy as people who suffer, and to stay loyal to the people who make a home with you even when the institutions over you fail.

delivery.evidence: Wikipedia notes the Order is later shown morally unclear and the Noah show hidden depths; no review found calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its message about grief and mercy rides on the premise itself, and both the Order and the Noah get sympathetic and cruel members.

personified.ideology: Mercy for every soul; keep walking
Grief turned into war on God and the world

entry.dominant: Christian (setting and reworked imagery), Dharmic-style non-attachment (my own framing), Classical virtue ethics, Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued), Existentialism.

series.title: Blue Exorcist
series.warning: Chapter 77 shows hypnotically forced sexual contact involving a 15-year-old; the story frames it as abuse.

entry.heading: Blue Exorcist
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is chosen, not inherited: you are not your father's blood. Loving the family that raised you, trusting your friends and protecting people, including the outcasts and the demons who do no harm, is what makes you human.

delivery.evidence: Kato: "There isn't a 'high' message in it" (ANN, 2011). StoryScanner: it "does not overtly mock Christian faith." No review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its messages about choosing your own path and accepting outsiders come through character arcs, while each faction, including the Order and the Illuminati, has both sympathetic and cruel members.

personified.ideology: Purity by force; hatred of demon blood
Immortality and a new order through science

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Communitarianism, Classical virtue ethics, Pagan / occult, Christian (as setting).

series.title: Sun-Ken Rock
series.warning: Sources report a 16-year-old character having sex with an adult and a 15-year-old doing porn work; whether these are drawn is unconfirmed.

entry.heading: Sun-Ken Rock
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is to use your strength to protect the weak and keep faith with the people who follow you, to judge people by their souls rather than by what has been done to their bodies, and in the end to let go of revenge.

content.framing: Mixed: protective violence endorsed; cruelty condemned
Sexual violence condemned in the story; fan service endorsed

delivery.evidence: Silverman says the Vietnam War discussions clash with the tone; reviewers quote "The state is just a gang that is legalized." No review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its ideas about the state, war guilt and protection come through speeches and backstories set inside a pulp gang story, and villains are given motives but abusers are drawn flatly.

personified.ideology: Strength exists to protect the weak
Gangs and countries are the same; pragmatic power
Revenge on a society that wronged the powerless
Law-and-order cop who becomes a yakuza heir

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (a warrior's code), Might makes right (explored), Communitarianism (gang as family), Pragmatism, Critical theory-style social critique (my own framing).

series.title: Tomodachi Game
series.warning: A 17-year-old is forced to strip and is photographed for blackmail, and her backstory includes sexual assault.

entry.heading: Tomodachi Game
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life puts friends before money and keeps trusting them even when every rule rewards betrayal, but the story also shows that the one who protects his friends best may be the most dangerous liar among them, and that he owes a full reckoning for what he has done.

content.framing: Mixed: exploitation condemned; fan service endorsed

delivery.evidence: ANN critics say villains' monologues constantly explain the plot ("tell-don't-show") and call the observers caricatures; no review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The friends-over-money motto is stated outright and repeated, while the game's cynical view of people is voiced at length by hosts and observers.

personified.ideology: Friends over money, by any means
Truth at any cost, even betrayal
People are products; despair is entertainment

entry.dominant: Communitarianism (friends as the highest good), Consumerism (critiqued: money as the measure of people), Pragmatism (cunning as the way through), Might makes right (explored and critiqued), Utilitarianism (the games' logic).

series.title: I Am a Hero
series.warning: The 35-year-old lead has sex with a high-school girl.

entry.heading: I Am a Hero
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: The story questions the idea of the hero: an ordinary, fearful man survives a collapsing society mostly by luck, and what it holds up as good is small acts of care and empathy, including empathy for the infected, rather than heroic deeds. It leaves the reader asking whether surviving is the same as living well.

content.framing: Mixed: sexual slavery is shown as abuse; the lead's sexual acts with Oda and with Hiromi are framed as romance or comfort

delivery.evidence: Dark Horse's editor says Hanazawa "played us" about who the hero is; no review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its themes come through irony and events rather than speeches, and the title's claim to heroism is left for the reader to judge.

personified.ideology: The ordinary man who imagines himself a hero
Empathy toward the other, even the infected
Order by force in a survivor community

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Absurdism, Nihilism, Collectivism / authoritarianism (critiqued), Might makes right (critiqued).

series.title: Kubo Won't Let Me Be Invisible
series.native: 久保さんは僕を許さない

entry.heading: Kubo Won't Let Me Be Invisible (Nene Yukimori)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life begins when someone truly sees you: being noticed and valued by one person can give a quiet, overlooked boy friends, joy and, in the end, the courage to say what he feels.

content.frequency: Romance central; mild fan service occasional

delivery.evidence: Reviewers call it "pure fluff" and "dirt simple" (ANN); no opened review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The idea that everyone deserves to be seen is carried by sight gags and small daily moments rather than stated lessons.

personified.ideology: Every overlooked person deserves to be seen

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Communitarianism, Expressive individualism (all weak; my own framing).

series.title: Tomie
series.warning: In chapter 1 a 15-year-old is in a sexual relationship with her adult teacher (sourcing is thin).

entry.heading: Tomie
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: The story promotes no good life. It shows desire for beauty and possession as a force that turns people into murderers, and it offers no cure; the few who survive are those who are not drawn in, such as a boy who prefers a plain girl and a man still faithful to his dead girlfriend.

delivery.evidence: Anime Feminist and Berlatsky say men's violence is framed sympathetically and Tomie is blamed; Taylor (via Wikipedia) reads it as critique.
delivery.note: The stories argue nothing outright; how fairly they treat women and men is the main point readers dispute.

entry.dominant: Feminism (contested), Nihilism, Hedonism (critiqued).

entry.heading: Fly Me to the Moon (Kenjiro Hata)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is a faithful, everyday marriage: two people who commit first and then learn to love each other through small daily kindnesses, so that even an endless, lonely life can find a home.

content.frequency: Romance central; fan service and innuendo occasional
content.framing: Romance endorsed; fan service and innuendo comic

delivery.evidence: Critics call it cute, funny and slow ("sufficiently cute and funny," ANN; "charming and refreshing," Anime UK News); none calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The value of committed marriage is shown through daily comedy rather than stated, and Chitose's opposition is treated with sympathy before she changes her mind.

personified.ideology: Longing for home and for a mortal life

entry.dominant: Traditionalism (marriage-centered), Existentialism (immortality and meaning), Classical virtue ethics (all moderate or weak; my own framing).

series.title: Alice in Borderland
series.adult_reason: Alice in Borderland: shown with a warning; VIZ rates it Mature (18+, VIZ Signature); attempted sexual assault of a high-school girl and sexual relationships involving high-school characters (fan wiki, Japanese Wikipedia, Mangapedia); deep entry scores 9
series.warning: Includes two attempted sexual assaults on a high-school girl and an adult woman seducing a high-school boy; the teen leads also have sex.

entry.heading: Alice in Borderland
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is chosen, not found: Arisu goes from wanting to escape his life to fighting to keep it, carried first by the friends who died for him and then by his love for Usagi. The story treats the will to live as something people hand to each other, and treats despair, cynicism and the Beach's pleasure-seeking as dead ends.

content.framing: Assault condemned; consensual sex not critiqued

delivery.evidence: AniList reviewers call it a reflection on "what is the meaning of life"; no opened review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Most of the theme comes through games and deaths, but ch. 43, ch. 62 and the final chapter state the argument openly, with Mira given a full case for giving up.

personified.ideology: Life is worth choosing for others' sake
Humans are predators; revel in it

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Nihilism (critiqued), Secular humanism, Communitarianism.

series.title: Dead Dead Demon's Dededede Destruction
series.native: デッドデッドデーモンズデデデデデストラクション

entry.heading: Dead Dead Demon's Dededede Destruction
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life holds onto one true bond and keeps seeing the human face in people others call enemies. Leaders, media and crowds that turn fear into hatred and profit are not to be trusted, and wanting to be the hero who saves the world can be more dangerous than choosing to save one person.

delivery.evidence: MAL reviewer: "a bit on the nose"; another says skip "the news talk and political pseudo-speech." No opened review calls it preachy; Solrad calls the politics "an undercurrent." Asano said in 2014 that after the 2011 earthquake "I decided that I didn't want to ever be preachy" (mangabrog translation). The Outer Haven (vol. 6) notes factions within the government, both protest camps and the invaders themselves.
delivery.note: The politics come through constant TV news, online chatter and protest scenes around the girls, while the leads themselves mostly joke about it.

personified.ideology: Wanting to save the world, believing in an "absolute"

entry.dominant: Critical theory, Existentialism, Absurdism, Nihilism (explored), Progressivism.

series.title: Shikimori's Not Just a Cutie
series.native: 可愛いだけじゃない式守さん

entry.heading: Shikimori's Not Just a Cutie (Keigo Maki)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is a partnership in which each person protects, supports and openly accepts the other as they are: love does not erase weakness or bad luck, but shares it, and frees both people from narrow ideas of what a boy or a girl should be.

content.frequency: Romance central; mild fan service rare

delivery.evidence: ANN says it is "having a conversation with gender norms"; Anime Feminist says it "explicitly addresses and rejects many gender role expectations."
delivery.note: The message about shared strength is carried by the comedy of role reversal and a few explicit talks, while Shikimori's wish to be cute and Kamiya's feelings are treated with sympathy rather than mocked.

personified.ideology: A woman can be both cute and strong; love as protection

entry.dominant: Feminism (gender-role reversal), Classical virtue ethics, Communitarianism (all moderate or weak; partly my own framing).

entry.heading: Given
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is lived by facing loss honestly and turning it into something you can give others. Love and friendship carry a person through grief, and you cannot hold another person by force.

content.framing: Endorsed (romance); Condemned (the forced advance); Mixed (the vol. 7 scene)

delivery.evidence: Reviewers praise emotional resonance and realism (ANN; OutWrite; AIPT); no reviewer found calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Different views of love (possessive, patient, free) get fair voices. Hurtful straight views of gay attraction appear in vol. 6 as hurtful, and no religious or traditional objection is voiced.

personified.ideology: Possessive devotion that must be outgrown

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Secular humanism, Progressivism, Expressive individualism.

entry.heading: Blue Flag
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is honest about who you are and whom you love, even when others' expectations and prejudice push you to hide; the choices you make at eighteen do not have to be final.

content.framing: Endorsed (romance); Neutral on orientation as a fact of life

delivery.evidence: ANN calls vol. 7 "more heavy-handed than it perhaps needs to be"; But Why Tho says the cringe-worthy prejudiced talk is there "because this is real."
delivery.note: The message is carried mostly by long conversations among the friends, becoming most direct after the confession (vols. 6-7).

personified.ideology: Being true to whom you love despite prejudice
Girls and boys can be friends; against sexist double standards
Rigid gender roles and anti-gay views

entry.dominant: Expressive individualism (being true to yourself), Progressivism (critique of prejudice and gender norms), Existentialism (choosing a future).

entry.heading: Billy Bat
entry.label: From summaries

delivery.evidence: An AniList reviewer calls it "a message to humanity"; ANN says it uses the thriller "to say something less conventional and more controversial." No review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The series argues through plot, history and the bat's direct speeches to its chosen artists rather than through narration.

personified.ideology: Artistic honesty and protection of the weak
A hidden "administrator" of history who judges humans foolish
Ownership of stories for profit and power

entry.dominant: Postmodernism (metafiction), Pantheist / New Age (a cosmic guiding entity), Might makes right (critiqued), Consumerism (critiqued), Christian (reinterpreted).

series.title: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure Part 5: Golden Wind
series.romaji: JoJo no Kimyou na Bouken: Ougon no Kaze
series.native: ジョジョの奇妙な冒険 黄金の風

entry.heading: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure Part 5: Golden Wind
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: You cannot change your fate, but you can refuse to give up your sense of right: loyalty to friends who chose the same path, protection of the weak against those who prey on them, and the courage to walk that road to its end are what make a life golden, even inside a criminal world.

content.framing: Shown with consequences (heroes' killings largely endorsed)

delivery.evidence: MAL reviewers say Diavolo is "barely even shown"; TV Tropes says fans root for the rebel assassins.
delivery.note: The anti-drug and fate themes come through characters' choices and backstories rather than speeches, while the main villain's view is barely argued.

personified.ideology: Seize power within a corrupt order to make it just
Absolute power through secrecy; erase the past at any cost
Revolt against the Boss for a fair share

entry.dominant: Stoicism (affirmed, through Araki's fate theme), Classical virtue ethics (affirmed), Communitarianism (affirmed, the crew as family), Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued, through the Boss), Might makes right (explored).

series.title: The 100 Girlfriends Who Really, Really, Really, Really, Really Love You
series.romaji: Kimi no Koto ga Dai Dai Dai Dai Daisuki na 100-nin no Kanojo
series.native: 君のことが大大大大大好きな100人の彼女
series.adult_reason: The 100 Girlfriends: shown with a warning; Seven Seas publishes it as Mature-rated (Ghost Ship imprint, Seven Seas' Mature tier = 18+); BBFC and Australian MA 15+ describe sexualized focus on teen characters in the anime; adult principal and teachers date a high-school student
series.warning: Most of the cast are high-school and junior-high students (ages 12-16); the anime is officially classed as sexualizing teen girls, adult school staff are written as partners of the 15-year-old lead, and an adult's forced kissing of students is a running gag.

entry.heading: The 100 Girlfriends Who Really, Really, Really, Really, Really Love You (Rikito Nakamura, Yukiko Nozawa)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life means being honest with everyone you care about and making room for each person exactly as she is. Belonging is not scarce: a group grows stronger when no one is forced to compete or left out.

content.framing: Endorsed (the group arrangement); fan service played for comedy

delivery.evidence: Rentaro states the thesis in speeches (Guinness-record speech; ANN quotes "Who ever said that loving someone means your love for someone else is fake?").
delivery.note: The story states its case for shared love openly through Rentaro's speeches, but wraps it in absurdist parody, so readers differ on how seriously to take it.

entry.dominant: Expressive individualism, Communitarianism, Hedonism.

publishers.name: Seven Seas
publishers.notes: 2  Omnibuses - Complete; print | 7 Vols - Complete; digital

entry.heading: orange
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is one where you speak up for the people you love before it is too late. Regret can be turned into care, friends can carry someone through despair, and a person in pain is worth staying alive for and with.

delivery.evidence: ANN calls it "emotionally gripping throughout"; Mage in a Barrel says it "never fetishizes his struggle"; no review found calling it preachy.
delivery.note: The letters state the lesson directly at times, but the message mostly works through Naho's choices and Kakeru's inner chapter rather than speeches.

personified.ideology: His death would make amends to his mother
True love puts the other's happiness first
Speak now, or live with regret
Regret can be sent back as help

entry.dominant: Communitarianism, Secular humanism, Existentialism.

series.title: Neon Genesis Evangelion
series.native: 新世紀エヴァンゲリオン
series.warning: Includes nudity of 14-year-old Rei and a scene where 14-year-old Asuka undresses in front of an adult man, who turns her down; the story does not frame either as sexual approval.

entry.heading: Neon Genesis Evangelion (manga)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life means choosing to live among other people, with the pain that comes from being separate, rather than escaping into isolation or into a merged, painless collective. Facing others, and your own fear, is worth the hurt.

content.framing: Neutral (fan service); Condemned (Kaworu's advances; Kaji turns Asuka down)

delivery.evidence: No review calls it preachy; CBR says Sadamoto gives "everything a concrete reason in-text"; Kotaku notes added inner thoughts.
delivery.note: Characters state the themes in dialogue and inner monologue, while the villains' plans are given motives.

personified.ideology: Grief turned into will to power

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Secular humanism, Transhumanism (critiqued), Collectivism (critiqued).

series.title: My Love Story with Yamada-kun at Lv999
series.romaji: Yamada-kun to Lv999 no Koi wo Suru
series.native: 山田くんとLv999の恋をする

entry.heading: My Love Story with Yamada-kun at Lv999
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is found by getting back up after being hurt, letting people in, and choosing a partner who is quietly faithful and honest. Online friends can become real friends, but trust has to be earned.

delivery.evidence: Reviewers praise "mature communication" and genre comfort (Anime Corner; But Why Tho); none calls it preachy or moralizing.
delivery.note: Its points about faithfulness and online trust come through comic situations and Akane's inner monologue rather than speeches.

personified.ideology: Quiet loyalty and honesty over charm
Caution and care for others online

entry.dominant: Communitarianism (the guild as chosen family), Classical virtue ethics (faithfulness and care), Expressive individualism (following one's feelings across an age gap).

series.title: Black Butler
series.warning: Black Butler (vol. 27, ch. 135-136) depicts, non-explicitly, the sexual abuse of ten-year-old twins by a cult; the series also contains child trafficking, ritual child murder and suggestive framing of its 12-to-13-year-old protagonist.

entry.heading: Black Butler
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: The story honors a life lived by one's own word and pride to the bitter end. Ciel refuses pity and forgiveness, trades his soul for revenge, and keeps the bargain. The story admires his resolve, condemns the people who prey on children, and shows the price he pays in his own humanity.

content.framing: Shown with consequences (villains); ambiguous (Ciel's own orders)

delivery.evidence: No review calls it preachy. Beasi (Manga Bookshelf) finds "a deeper story" under a "fairly vapid" start; the OASG calls the darkness "not gratuitous."
delivery.note: The series rarely states a moral; its view emerges through Ciel's choices and the fates of villains, with the hero's revenge left largely unjudged.

personified.ideology: Death and its reversal as entertainment

entry.dominant: Pagan / occult, Might makes right (revenge), Traditionalism, Nihilism.

series.title: Welcome to Demon School! Iruma-kun
series.native: 魔入りました！入間くん

entry.heading: Welcome to Demon School! Iruma-kun
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is a kind one shared with people who love you: let yourself be cared for, care for others in return, learn what you actually want, and grow by effort, without becoming cruel.

content.framing: Neutral (comic and contest fights); condemned when villains do it

delivery.evidence: ANN says it works "serious themes under its sillier elements"; ScreenWise calls it "really wholesome." No review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Lessons about kindness and self-worth ride under gag comedy, while the hidden villains are given motives but framed as sadistic or destructive.

personified.ideology: Pleasure in despair; overturn the rank order by force

entry.dominant: Communitarianism (found family), Classical virtue ethics, Expressive individualism (learning to want), Confucian ethics.

series.title: Prison School
series.adult_reason: Prison School: shown with a warning; Yen Press rates it 18+ M (Mature); MangaUpdates genre Adult; BBFC and Australian MA 15+ describe sexualised imagery of a high-school cast in the anime
series.warning: Prison School (manga) repeatedly shows its 15-year-old protagonist nude and in sexualized fetish scenes with other high-school students, played for comedy.

entry.heading: Prison School (Akira Hiramoto)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life means standing by your friends through any humiliation, keeping your word, and never giving up hope of escape; rigid authority and the war between the sexes are absurd, and loyalty is what survives them.

content.framing: Played for comedy; voyeurism punished but punishments are themselves sexualized

delivery.evidence: ANN's Creamer: cast "utterly without dignity", "every single person deserves what happens to them"; AIPT: "knows exactly what it is."
delivery.note: The story makes almost no stated argument; both student councils and the boys are caricatured, and loyalty is shown through action.

personified.ideology: Female authority; males should be expelled

entry.dominant: Hedonism, Absurdism, Libertarianism.

series.title: Kimi ni Todoke: From Me to You

entry.heading: Kimi ni Todoke: From Me to You
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life comes from reaching out to others with sincerity and patience: kindness, honest words and loyal friends can undo loneliness and misunderstanding, and love grows best slowly and with respect.

delivery.evidence: Common Sense Media and ScreenWise name kindness and empathy as messages; no opened review calls it preachy. Rivals get motives and apologies.
delivery.note: The message is mostly shown through Sawako's slow change, with some direct statements in her narration and her graduation speech.

personified.ideology: Sincerity and patience over social status
Blunt, worldly realism with care underneath

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Communitarianism, Confucian ethics, Secular humanism.

series.title: More Than a Married Couple, but Not Lovers.

entry.heading: More Than a Married Couple, but Not Lovers. (Yuki Kanamaru)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: Love is learned by living alongside someone: by showing up, telling the truth about your feelings and choosing the person who actually knows you over the idealized crush.

content.framing: Endorsed (romance); Neutral (fan service, sex jokes); Condemned (harassment by strangers)

delivery.evidence: ANN: romance "surprisingly wholesome" despite an "Orwellian" premise; Anime Feminist: wastes the premise, no commentary. No review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its point about love growing through shared life comes through the cohabitation and the confessions, while the programme and the fan service go largely unexamined.

entry.dominant: Expressive individualism, Hedonism, Communitarianism.

publishers.name: Viz
publishers.notes: 2 Volume - Complete | 1 Volume Perfect Edition - Complete

entry.heading: 21st Century Boys
entry.label: From summaries

delivery.evidence: Reviewers stress memory, "falsified truth," a "humane" ending; none calls it preachy. Urasawa says he avoids presenting shifting values of good and evil (Sankei 2017).
delivery.note: The conclusion makes its point about confession through a mystery reveal and a childhood flashback rather than speeches.

personified.ideology: Owning up to one's own past wrongs
Resentment of the excluded turned into a will to destroy
A new generation that refuses its father's legacy

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Existentialism, Secular humanism, Communitarianism, Collectivism / authoritarianism (critiqued).

series.title: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure Part 2: Battle Tendency
series.romaji: JoJo no Kimyou na Bouken: Sentou Chouryuu
series.native: ジョジョの奇妙な冒険 戦闘潮流

entry.heading: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure Part 2: Battle Tendency
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is lived with wit, courage and loyalty to friends and family, carrying on what those before you gave. Cleverness and humor can beat raw power, and a friend's sacrifice is honored by finishing the fight.

delivery.evidence: ANN says the respect-across-differences message is "hammered in a bit too hard"; ComicsAlliance calls the Nazi rescue "morally empty."
delivery.note: The message comes through action and friendship rather than speeches; Wamuu gets a warrior's dignity, Stroheim gets redemption by courage without renouncing his cause, and Kars's view of humans as food is never given a serious hearing.

personified.ideology: Wit and trickery over strength; family pride
Domination; become a perfect being with no weakness
Nazi national pride; "Only the great should live"

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (affirmed), Pragmatism (affirmed through Joseph), Communitarianism (affirmed), Traditionalism (affirmed), Might makes right and Transhumanism (critiqued through Kars).

series.title: Our Dreams at Dusk: Shimanami Tasogare
series.warning: Contains a scene in which a sixth-grade character is groped by a stranger at a festival (ch. 9); the story treats it as wrong.

entry.heading: Our Dreams at Dusk: Shimanami Tasogare
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life comes from finding a place where you can be who you are, slowly and in your own words, among people who accept you; no one has to fully understand themselves, and community, not labels, is what keeps a person alive.

delivery.evidence: ANN's Silverman finds some symbolism "a bit too on the nose"; TV Tropes YMMV lists Anvilicious; a MyAnimeList user review calls it message-driven.
delivery.note: Homophobic voices are shown as ordinary people capable of change, but no character voices a principled religious or traditional objection.

entry.dominant: Progressivism, Communitarianism, Expressive individualism.

series.title: My Lesbian Experience With Loneliness
series.romaji: Sabishisugite Rezu Fuzoku ni Ikimashita Report
series.native: さびしすぎてレズ風俗に行きましたレポ

entry.heading: My Lesbian Experience With Loneliness
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life starts with treating yourself as worth caring for: stop living for others' approval, tell the truth about what you feel, and take small, concrete steps toward the work and connection you actually want.

content.frequency: Central premise; one main encounter (ch. 4), the opening (ch. 1) and a later visit

delivery.evidence: WWAC says it "never felt weepy or overwrought"; The OASG finds the parents underdeveloped; the author later regretted her portrayal of them.
delivery.note: The author states her lessons directly as narration, while her parents' view of a good life is shown only from her side.

entry.dominant: Expressive individualism, Secular humanism, Existentialism.

series.title: Maid-sama!
series.warning: Contains two attempted sexual assaults on the 16-year-old heroine, both stopped: two men bind and gag her in a café (ch. 3), and a rival school's president pins her down and tries to force a kiss (ch. 8).

entry.heading: Maid-sama!
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is earned through hard work and honest effort: you carry your family when you must, stand up for those weaker than you, and learn that accepting help and love does not make you weak.

content.framing: Mixed: romance endorsed; the attempted assaults and villains' advances condemned; some of Usui's pushiness played as romantic

delivery.evidence: SLJ says it turns gender roles in unexpected directions; Draper Carlson calls it "a male fantasy"; no review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Messages about work, equality and accepting help are shown through Misaki's choices and occasional speeches, inside a broad comedy.

personified.ideology: Self-reliance and equal rules for girls and boys
Privilege that thinks money buys people

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Feminism, Confucian ethics, Expressive individualism.

series.title: Yokohama Kaidashi Kikou
series.native: ヨコハマ買い出し紀行

entry.heading: Yokohama Kaidashi Kikou (Yokohama Shopping Log)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is lived slowly and attentively: savoring small, everyday beauty, keeping friendships, and accepting that people, places and even humanity pass away.

delivery.evidence: Nicoll: "more about savouring moments than answering questions"; Okazu: "no real plot." No review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The series has no antagonists or argued positions; its outlook is carried by mood, pacing and what it chooses to show.

personified.ideology: Contentment and attention to the present moment
Striving and going out into the world
Accepting age and death with grace

entry.dominant: Dharmic (Buddhist impermanence), Stoicism, Naturalism, Secular humanism.

series.title: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure Part 4: Diamond is Unbreakable
series.romaji: JoJo no Kimyou na Bouken: Diamond wa Kudakenai
series.native: ジョジョの奇妙な冒険 ダイヤモンドは砕けない

entry.heading: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure Part 4: Diamond Is Unbreakable
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is ordinary life shared with friends and neighbours, worth defending when evil hides behind a normal face. In Araki's words, "true strength is found in not doing bad things" (Wikipedia).

delivery.evidence: Viz calls it "a fun little murder mystery"; ANN's Hopper says perversity is "reveled in" but campy.
delivery.note: The message comes through the town's slow discovery of the killer rather than speeches; Kira explains his "quiet life" philosophy in his own words, and the story answers it by his fate.

personified.ideology: Protect the town and the people in it
A quiet, private life at any cost to others
Art and curiosity above ordinary morality

entry.dominant: Communitarianism (affirmed), Classical virtue ethics (affirmed), Hedonism (critiqued through Kira), Expressive individualism (explored through Rohan and Josuke's style).

publishers.name: Kodansha USA
publishers.notes: 12 Digital Volumes; Ongoing | 12 Physicals Singles; Ongoing | 2 [3-in-1] Physical Omnibuses; Ongoing

entry.heading: A Sign of Affection (Yubisaki to Renren)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is lived in honest connection: learning another person's language, saying what you feel, accepting help without being defined by it, and choosing a partner who widens your world, then committing to that partner for life. Disability is part of an ordinary, full life, not the whole of it.

delivery.evidence: Creators say they avoided "an overly moralistic angle" (Sakuga Blog); ANN, But Why Tho and OASG note it explains deafness only as the story needs.
delivery.note: The inclusion message is carried by Yuki's point of view, lettering and everyday scenes rather than speeches, with Oushi's protective view given its own chapters.

personified.ideology: Openness: meet every person in their own language
Deaf people need to be protected from the hearing world
Disability is part of an ordinary, self-directed life

entry.dominant: Secular humanism, Progressivism (disability inclusion), Expressive individualism.

series.title: The Dangers in My Heart
series.romaji: Boku no Kokoro no Yabai Yatsu

entry.heading: The Dangers in My Heart
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life opens up when a person stops sneering at the world from a distance and lets others in. Seeing the good in other people, and learning to be kind and honest about one's own feelings, is shown as the way out of self-hatred and loneliness.

delivery.evidence: Eisenbeis (ANN) notes a "great message about growing up"; no review found calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The message grows out of Kyotaro's inner monologue and slow change rather than speeches, and rivals such as Adachi are treated as decent people.

personified.ideology: Contempt for the social world; violent edgy fantasy
Openness and seeing the good in others

entry.dominant: Secular humanism (empathy and growth), Classical virtue ethics (kindness, courage, honesty), Existentialism (self-making), with Nihilism and edgy misanthropy critiqued.

series.title: The Case Study of Vanitas
series.warning: The Case Study of Vanitas (vol. 9, Mémoire 47) states in a flashback that the child Mikhail was forced by his mother into sexual services for her customers while dressed as a girl; it is told rather than drawn, and the series also shows experiments on children, beheadings and suicide attempts.

entry.heading: The Case Study of Vanitas
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life faces its own shortness honestly, refuses to treat anyone, human or vampire, as a thing, and lets itself be loved even when it does not feel deserving. Hatred, revenge and purity crusades on either side destroy the people they claim to protect.

content.framing: Mixed: the forced kiss is played partly as comedy

delivery.evidence: TV Tropes calls the Paladins an "extremist religious group"; But Why Tho says Roland is "less black and white." No review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: Its themes of identity and mortality come through plot and symbols, while the Church's orders appear mostly through violent members given sympathetic backstories.

personified.ideology: Self-hatred and mercy driven by revenge

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Classical virtue ethics, Christian (as heritage, with the institution critiqued), Postmodernism, Communitarianism.

series.title: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure Part 3: Stardust Crusaders
series.romaji: JoJo no Kimyou na Bouken: Stardust Crusaders
series.native: ジョジョの奇妙な冒険スターダストクルセイダース
series.warning: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure Part 3: Stardust Crusaders, ch. 18: partial nudity of a child character (Anne, a runaway girl) in a shower scene and an attempted sexual assault on her by a villain.

entry.heading: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure Part 3: Stardust Crusaders
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life protects its family and friends, faces evil without flinching, and is ready to give everything for others; the bloodline's "heritage for the future" is courage passed on, not power.

delivery.evidence: ANN calls the anime "beautifully stupid" with "an ignorant and infectious glee"; reviewers praise fights, not messages.
delivery.note: The message comes through sacrifice and fights rather than speeches; Dio voices his view of fear and power in his own words, while most assassins are one-note hired killers.

personified.ideology: Rule by fear; power to escape fear and death

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (affirmed), Might makes right (critiqued through Dio), Pagan/occult (explored as imagery), Traditionalism (family lineage, affirmed).

entry.heading: Hajime no Ippo: Fighting Spirit!
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: Strength is not the power to hurt others but the courage to keep stepping forward. A bullied, gentle boy earns his place through relentless work, honors every opponent, and learns that the ring costs the body something real, and then that strength can also mean teaching and protecting others.

content.framing: Mostly Neutral (sport within rules); street violence and fouls Condemned; brain damage Shown with consequences
Played for comedy; Takamura's groping treated as a gag (TV Tropes)

content.frequency: Pervasive outside the book; rare inside

delivery.evidence: ANN's reviewer says supporting characters "feel like real people"; Common Sense Media cites hard work and redemption themes.
delivery.note: The message comes through matches and training, and Takamura's harder view of strength is voiced by a beloved character rather than knocked down.

personified.ideology: Win at world level by giving up "humanity"

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Communitarianism, Stoicism; Might makes right explored and partly affirmed in the ring, critiqued outside it.

series.title: Innocent
series.adult_reason: Innocent: Dark Horse rates all three omnibuses 18+ (Violence, nudity, language); graphic torture and executions; sources report sexual abuse of a girl under 10 (content warning); deep entry scores 9
series.warning: Includes the sexual abuse of a nine-year-old girl by an adult official (likely vols. 5-6) and of a 14-year-old boy on his father's orders (vol. 1), alongside graphic torture and executions.

entry.heading: Innocent
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is to keep mercy and conscience alive inside a cruel duty you cannot escape: to see the condemned as human beings, to refuse cruelty for its own sake, and to hope for a justice that no longer kills.

content.framing: Abuse condemned; sex scenes neutral; eroticized suffering

delivery.evidence: No review calls it preachy; Farris finds the symbolism "a bit too grandiose"; Dacey calls the father "cartoonishly evil", "a foil" for Charles.
delivery.note: Its case against cruelty and the death penalty comes through Charles's suffering and the image of the crowd rather than speeches, while the opposing view (duty and order) is voiced mainly by harsh relatives and corrupt nobles.

personified.ideology: Radical freedom; defiance of God, King and patriarchy
Duty to the family office above the self

personified.character: Count de Chartois / Count de Luxe

entry.dominant: Existentialism (fate versus choice), Secular humanism (dignity of the condemned), Collectivism/authoritarianism (absolute monarchy, critiqued), Feminism (Marie-Joseph), Christian (Charles's faith and martyr imagery).

series.title: The Rising of the Shield Hero
series.native: 盾の勇者の成り上がり

entry.heading: The Rising of the Shield Hero
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is to protect the people in your care, endure injustice without becoming what wronged you, and rebuild trust one loyal companion at a time. The story pairs this with a strong appetite for public justice against those who abuse power, and it gives its hero the use of a slave system it does not fully examine.

content.framing: Mixed: the accusation is shown as a lie and punished; fan service and jokes are played as comedy

delivery.evidence: ANN calls the setup "enormously heavy-handed" railroading; ComicBook.com calls the accusation "a cheap shortcut." No review opened says strawman.
delivery.note: Its message about injustice and loyalty is stated through Naofumi's anger and the queen's verdict, while the villains are drawn with little inner life until the king's later redemption.

personified.ideology: Self-reliance after betrayal; protect your own

personified.character: High Priest of the Church of the Three Heroes

entry.dominant: Pragmatism, Classical virtue ethics, Might makes right (explored), Communitarianism. (Labels are my own framing unless a source is named.)

entry.heading: Dragon Ball Super (manga, 2015-present, on hiatus)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is joyful, unending striving: keep training past every limit, enjoy a worthy opponent, protect your family and friends, and give former enemies a seat at the table, even in a cosmos whose rulers can erase everything on a whim.

content.framing: Endorsed (fighting as joy and test), with mass death shown at a cosmic, mostly bloodless scale
Played for light romance or gag

delivery.evidence: Inferred from summaries; no review opened addresses preachiness. Reviewers focus on pacing and power creep.
delivery.note: Values come through fights and gags, while villains' ideologies (Zamasu's purge of mortals) are stated and defeated rather than debated.

lenses.label: Might makes right
lenses.stance: Explored (critiqued in villains, affirmed in plot mechanics and cosmic order)

series.title: Fruits Basket

publishers.notes: Expired / 23 Vols - Complete | 6 Ultimate Edition Vols - Incomplete

entry.heading: Fruits Basket
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life comes from accepting people as they are and being accepted in turn: love that does not cling or control can heal deep family wounds, and each person must choose to leave an unhealthy bond and walk on their own.

content.framing: Mixed (adult affairs shown as damaging; teen romances endorsed)

delivery.evidence: Takaya says she tries to include "some kind of message" and give "a conclusion" (Time, 2006); ANN calls vol. 16 "non-stop angst."
delivery.note: The message is carried by backstories and long inner monologues, with direct statements of the theme in Kyoko's and Tohru's words.

entry.heading: RuriDragon
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: Being different is not a barrier to belonging: a life is good when you stop hiding what you are, say honestly what you feel, and let friends, family and community meet you halfway.

content.frequency: Occasional, rising in the latest arc

delivery.evidence: Shindo states the message ("being different is interesting"); reviewers praise natural, unscripted dialogue; no review calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The message comes through everyday conversations, with a few direct speeches when Ruri addresses the school or the class (ch. 25, 38-40).

personified.ideology: Blunt honesty; judging by appearance, then correcting it
Protective oversight by a state agency

series.title: Memories of Emanon
series.warning: The opening pages and one panel show Emanon, a 17-year-old character, nude in non-sexual, symbolic images; she also smokes and drinks throughout.

entry.heading: Memories of Emanon
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is one lived attentively and remembered: a single honest meeting can matter for a lifetime, and every person is a brief, real part of a story of life far older and larger than themselves.

delivery.evidence: Reviewers stress mood, art and conversation, "philosophical sci-fi discussions" (Otaku USA); Anime UK News says the point is hard to discern.
delivery.note: Ideas are delivered through Emanon's long monologues about memory and evolution, but the story draws no moral and leaves the meaning open.

personified.ideology: Life as one continuous memory; wonder and weariness at deep time
Open-minded science-fiction romanticism that settles into ordinary life

entry.dominant: Naturalism, Existentialism, Environmentalism (light), Dharmic echoes (impermanence).

series.title: March Comes in Like a Lion

entry.heading: March Comes in Like a Lion
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is rebuilt through other people: grief and depression are not cured by talent or effort alone, but by letting others in, being cared for and caring in return, and finding a family where you can belong.

content.framing: Shown with consequences (affair); Endorsed (slow teen romance)
Shown with consequences (healed slowly through support)

delivery.evidence: Reviewers praise its psychological depth and humor (Manga Bookshelf; Anime Feminist); none opened calls it preachy. Antagonists get backstories.
delivery.note: The message comes through Rei's inner narration and the slow change in his relationships rather than speeches, though the narration is often reflective.

personified.ideology: Resentment as a response to neglect

entry.dominant: Communitarianism, Classical virtue ethics, Secular humanism, Existentialism.

series.title: We Never Learn
series.native: ぼくたちは勉強ができない
series.warning: Fan service includes partial nudity and sexualized scenes of named high-school girls (including a bath scene in chapter 15), and the hero's middle-school sister exposes herself to him as a joke.

entry.heading: We Never Learn (Bokutachi wa Benkyou ga Dekinai)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life comes from honest effort toward a goal you choose, even in your worst subject, and from helping others reach theirs; love and family grow out of that shared work.

content.framing: Endorsed (romance); Neutral or played for laughs (fan service)

delivery.evidence: Reviews call it formulaic harem comedy, not preachy (ANN Manga Guide). Mafuyu's talent-first view is given reasons and a backstory.
delivery.note: The effort message is stated through Nariyuki's father's motto and shown through exam results; the romance carries most of the weight.

personified.ideology: Follow your natural talent; emotions mislead

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics (diligence), Pragmatism, Confucian ethics, Hedonism (in the fan service).

series.title: Usogui
series.adult_reason: Usogui: deep entry scores violence 9 (torture executions, cannibalism); no publisher rating; content warning for a child-exploitation backstory.
