entry.heading: Usogui
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: It presents life as a gamble that everyone is already making: the good life belongs to those who see through lies, read people truly, stake everything on their own judgment and keep faith with the few companions they trust.

content.framing: Shown with consequences (and partly as spectacle)
Mixed (gambling and deception are the hero's tools)

delivery.evidence: AniList reviewer: every character "has a unique backstory without being too preachy"; another: fights are "battles between conflicting ideologies."
delivery.note: Ideas are carried by gamblers' rival philosophies and decided by the games, not stated as morals by a narrator.

personified.ideology: Life is a gamble; truth won by reading through lies
Revolutionary terror to purge a "corrupt" Japan; gamblers as "noxious insects" (ch. 36)
Order exists to protect the strong (fan wiki)

series.title: Please Go Home, Miss Akutsu!
series.native: 帰ってください! 阿久津さん

entry.heading: Please Go Home, Miss Akutsu! (Taichi Nagaoka)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is a warm, unhurried companionship: two awkward people who keep choosing each other's company, with family and friends cheering them on, find in an ordinary room the closeness they both lacked.

content.framing: Romance endorsed; fan service played for comedy (neutral)

delivery.evidence: Reviewers discuss pacing and charm; none calls it preachy (UK Anime Network; MyAnimeList reviews).
delivery.note: The view that patient companionship leads to love is carried by daily gags and the parents' parallel story, not stated lessons.

personified.ideology: Take what you want; tough outside, tender inside
Love grows from persistent closeness, as it did for us

series.title: Yamada-kun and the Seven Witches
series.warning: Played-for-comedy fan service includes nudity and partial nudity of named high-school characters (ages 16-18), such as bath and body-swap scenes in chapters 1-2 and 95; no sex scene is reported.

entry.heading: Yamada-kun and the Seven Witches
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life comes from letting other people in: a bored loner finds friends, purpose and love by helping others with their problems, and honest effort counts for more than shortcuts.

delivery.evidence: No review calls it preachy; Kotaku praises its comedy; rival councils and clubs get motives and redemption arcs.
delivery.note: The message about friendship and loyalty comes through plot and comedy, with a few direct statements in Yamada's reflections (ch. 88, 240).

personified.ideology: Loyalty and helping others over self-interest
Getting back what you lost at any cost

entry.dominant: Communitarianism, Classical virtue ethics, Hedonism (as comedy), Pragmatism.

entry.heading: LIAR GAME
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: Honesty and trust, practiced with open eyes, can beat a system built on greed and fear: when players stop trying to profit from each other and cooperate, nobody has to be ruined.

delivery.evidence: Critics note the show "spells out its strategies"; Eisenbeis names the theme "idealism versus pragmatism"; Yokoya argues his case at length.
delivery.note: The theme is stated aloud in debates between Nao, Akiyama and Yokoya, but each rival's view gets clever play and real wins before it loses.

personified.ideology: Honesty and trust as the way to win
Rational doubt that leads to earned trust
Control through false religion and emotional dependence

series.title: My Broken Mariko
series.native: マイ・ブロークン・マリコ
series.warning: Includes a backstory of a girl's sexual abuse by her father in childhood and adolescence, stated rather than shown, and centers on her suicide.

entry.heading: My Broken Mariko
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: Grief and guilt after a suicide cannot be solved, only lived through: the one thing the living can do for the dead is go on living, and the love of one true friend matters even when it could not save her.

content.framing: Shown with consequences (grief; choosing to live)

delivery.evidence: Reviewers stress it does not lecture: "doesn't seek to educate us or convey a clear message" (AniList review); Bleeding Cool says it skips social commentary.
delivery.note: The message is carried by Shiino's grief and one stranger's plain words, while the abuser is a figure of menace with no point of view.

personified.ideology: Keep living for the sake of the dead

entry.heading: BECK

entry.life_message: A good life is found by finding something to love and working at it with friends who will not let you quit: music, practice and loyalty turn a boy who thinks he is nobody into someone who can move a crowd.

delivery.evidence: Reviewers praise its honesty and realism (ANN; AnimeOnDVD via Wikipedia); none calls it preachy. Industry villains are one-sided.

entry.life_message: A good life is lived openly and honestly among others: reaching out to people across social lines, being yourself without pretense, and letting friends and family support you lets each person heal and grow.

delivery.evidence: ANN's Silverman praises how it treats characters as individuals; ANN's This Week in Anime calls it "deceptively easy," Nao's story "not all idealized."
delivery.note: Values come through characters' small choices and inner monologue, and even the antagonists (Mika, Chieri, Shima's mother) get reasons and a chance to change.

series.title: Parasyte

entry.heading: Parasyte
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life means holding on to human feeling (grief, tears, mercy and care for others) while facing honestly that humans are one predatory species among many, with no special right over the Earth; love and mercy, not reason alone, are what make us human.

content.framing: Mixed: teen sex shown as tender; crimes condemned

delivery.evidence: Comics Worth Reading praises its ethics questions; Iwaaki said he did not want to "look down on humans"; Hirokawa's environmentalism is voiced fully, then questioned.

entry.heading: Blade of the Immortal

series.title: Insomniacs After School

entry.heading: Insomniacs After School
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is found by sharing your fears honestly with people who will stay with you: two lonely teenagers who cannot face the night find rest, purpose and love by keeping each other company, taking up a craft with patience, and choosing to live fully in spite of illness.

delivery.evidence: Reviewers call it "grounded," "quiet," "low-key"; Anime Feminist says it "respects her beyond being a love interest." No review calls it preachy.

series.title: Inside Mari

entry.heading: Inside Mari

entry.life_message: A self cannot be borrowed or escaped into: the way out of loneliness is to be seen as you are by someone who looks, and to face your own history rather than hide inside an imagined other.

content.framing: Shown with consequences (as symptom of crisis)

delivery.evidence: Reviewers stress mystery and ambiguity; Dupree says it shows Komori as an honest portrait of a predatory gaze, not a lecture. None calls it preachy.
delivery.note: The message emerges through the twist and the art (faceless figures, mirrors) rather than through speeches.

A parent's control over a child's identity

entry.heading: Takopi's Original Sin

entry.life_message: Real help starts with listening to and understanding another person's pain, not with magic fixes; children are broken by what adults do to them, and no single person is to blame.

entry.heading: Death Note: a-Kira (Tsugumi Ohba and Takeshi Obata)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: The chapter shows a world in which the power to kill becomes merchandise: a clever boy who will not kill sells the means to whoever pays most, governments bid while promising not to use it, and the seller dies by a rule he could not foresee. It holds out cleverness and money as hollow answers, and leaves death, and Ryuk's boredom, as the only constants.

delivery.evidence: The Mary Sue says it "hits the nail on the head" on how governments would react; leaders are caricatures, but the president gets a shrewd move.
delivery.note: The chapter makes its point through plot irony (the seller dies on payment) rather than speeches, though its leaders are drawn as caricatures of real people.

personified.ideology: Clever self-interest indifferent to how a weapon is used

entry.heading: Banana Fish
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: What it promotes as a good life: a life is measured by its bonds rather than its length; loyalty and a love that asks for nothing can give dignity to someone the world has used and hurt, but violence, even in a just cause, carries a cost that has to be paid.

delivery.note: Themes are carried by action and character rather than speeches, but the villains embody abuse and greed with little inner life.

personified.ideology: Freedom from ownership at any cost

entry.heading: Pluto: Urasawa x Tezuka
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: Hatred, not machines, is the real danger. A good life refuses revenge, grieves honestly, cares for the people (and robots) close at hand, and chooses to end the cycle of hate rather than win it.

delivery.evidence: Thompson (ANN) calls the politics "so heavy-handed"; This Week in Anime calls it "that blatant" approvingly; A.V. Club calls it frank.
delivery.note: The anti-war and anti-hatred message is stated openly through the Iraq-war parallels and characters' speeches, inside a slow murder mystery.

personified.ideology: Forgiveness ends the cycle of hate

entry.dominant: Secular humanism, Transhumanism (explored), Progressivism, Dharmic (Buddhist echo on hatred), Collectivism / authoritarianism (critiqued).
